#4995. Decrypt Becomes First News Publisher to Offer Perps Trading, Powered by Solana's Phoenix

Decrypt Becomes First News Publisher to Offer Perps Trading, Powered by Solana's Phoenix

What happens when the place you read the news becomes the place you act on it?

The news that moves markets and the tools to trade them have long lived in separate places. Decrypt is bringing them together.

Decrypt is integrating perpetual futures trading, powered by Phoenix, a fully onchain perpetuals exchange on Solana, making it the first media platform to offer perps trading directly alongside its journalism.

Readers will be able to take long or short positions on crypto, stocks and commodities from the same place they follow the news that moves them, without switching apps, connecting external wallets or moving funds between platforms.

"Information influences decisions, shapes opinions and moves markets," said Ilan Hazan, co-founder and COO of Decrypt. "A reader might discover an opportunity through a publication, develop a view and then leave to act on it somewhere else. The publisher monetizes the impression, while someone else monetizes the transaction. It means the publisher captures only a small part of the economic activity that its information and distribution generates."

Rather than treating media and financial products as separate businesses, he said, Decrypt is bringing them together. "We're allowing readers to go from understanding what's happening in the markets to taking a position, without leaving Decrypt.”

"Partnering with Decrypt closes the gap between reading the news and acting on it," said Kabir Sethi, Head of Business Development at Phoenix. "With over 100 Phoenix perpetuals markets built directly into Decrypt, readers can take in a story, form a view, and trade it in the same place. We are excited to help play a part in transforming Decrypt into a true information exchange."

Perpetual futures, or perps, are contracts that let traders bet on an asset's price rising or falling without an expiry date, typically using leverage. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses, and positions can be liquidated quickly when markets move against them.

Phoenix offers markets in crypto, U.S. stocks, gold and pre-IPO companies around the clock, with up to 40x leverage and low fees, according to its website. It is developed by Ellipsis Labs, a team that has built exclusively on Solana and whose CEO, Eugene Chen, has described perps as having "crazy product market fit."

"These are very, very strong, high revenue businesses, probably some of the best in the industry," Chen said of perps exchanges in a podcast interview with Blockworks' Lightspeed earlier this year. Phoenix routes each trade at the moment it lands onchain, splitting it between its order book and market makers "based on what's going to give you the best price," he explained.

Perps trading runs through the Decrypt Money Account, a single self-custodial account on Solana designed to work without seed phrases, gas fees or bridging.

One balance now funds it all: prediction markets on Decrypt Predict, Jupiter-powered token swaps, Earn and, now, perpetual futures. Users can also send funds privately, after Decrypt added confidential transfers through Solana infrastructure firm Helius.

Imagine reading about a public company's earnings and taking a position on its stock, at any hour. Or following a breaking story about Bitcoin and going long or short in the same moment.

From information to execution, in one place.

Announced in September, The Information Exchange is Decrypt's vision for the next generation of financial media: a single destination bringing together news, intelligence, market data, probabilities, direct financial participation—with perps forming the latest building block in that infrastructure.

News moves markets. Now readers can move with it.

Perpetual futures are leveraged products and carry a high risk of loss. Availability may vary by region.

#4992. OKX-ICE Tokenized Stock Venue Sets Launch, Turning to Crypto Companies After Big Tech Opts Out

OKX-ICE Tokenized Stock Venue Sets Launch, Turning to Crypto Companies After Big Tech Opts Out

After weeks of rejections from corporate America, OKX and ICE’s tokenized stock venue has found its launch lineup: crypto’s own public companies.

OKXICE said Wednesday that its Tokenized Securities Venue will open Nov. 23, letting eligible U.S. customers trade tokenized securities around the clock in the OKX app.

More than 70 assets are expected to be listed, including securities from Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood, Strategy, BitGo, Securitize and Better.com, plus 59 ETFs from Direxion. Strategy will also list its preferred stocks.

That’s a very different roster from the one the venue started with. As of its Nov. 5 notice, 67 companies, including every member of the “Magnificent Seven” tech giants, had objected to having their shares traded on the platform. Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy were notably absent from that list, and all three are now among the venue’s launch issuers.

“The SEC has created a real opening for American markets to lead the next era of finance,” said former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, who co-chairs OKXICE, a joint venture between OKX and NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange.

Securitize will provide the tokenization infrastructure. Each token represents an entitlement backed one-for-one by a real U.S. share, carrying dividends, voting rights and other shareholder benefits, according to the announcement.

Trading will run through automated market maker pools built on Uniswap v4 on X Layer, OKX’s Ethereum layer-2 network, and customers will hold their tokens in self-custodial wallets.

Strategy CEO Phong Le called tokenization on the venue “a natural next step” for the company’s preferred stocks, such as STRC.

Access is limited to eligible U.S.-based OKX customers who activate a CeDeFi Wallet, pass identity verification and complete onboarding with OKXICE. The venue operates under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate. Under the exemption, companies can keep third-party tokenized versions of their stock off a given venue by objecting within 30 days.

The launch caps a busy stretch for Wall Street tokenization. DTCC’s new tokenization service, which runs partly on the Canton Network, went live in late October, and Morgan Stanley said it was among the first banks to use it.

The position in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) was worth about $187 million on Sept. 30, up from $88.5 million for 2.66 million shares on June 30, according to Barclays’ Friday Form 13F filing.

“Early readings suggest longer-term holders make up a growing share of the spot bitcoin ETF investor base,” Bitwise analyst Camran Khosravi told Cointelegraph, pointing to increased bank exposure, including at Citigroup.

Citigroup reported a new position worth about $119 million in the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC). Its reported IBIT holdings also rose 50% to about 521,000 shares, from 347,000 at the end of June.

The filings offer an early indication of changing institutional Bitcoin ETF ownership, with more major banks and hedge funds yet to disclose their third-quarter positions. Institutional investment managers have until Monday to file their third-quarter holdings reports.

Banks accounted for $258 million, or 4.9%, of reported spot Bitcoin ETF holdings among early third-quarter filers, up from $107 million, or 3.2%, in Q2, according to Bitwise data shared with Cointelegraph.

Investment advisers remained the largest holders, accounting for $3.5 billion, or 66.6%, of reported positions, up from $2.2 billion in the previous quarter. Bitwise compared holdings across the two quarters for the 1,389 institutions that had filed their third-quarter reports by Friday. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETP) holdings of early Q3 2026 13F filers. Source: Bitwise

#4987. A High-Severity Bug Could Have Stalled Bitcoin Mining—Bitcoin Core Has a Fix

A High-Severity Bug Could Have Stalled Bitcoin Mining—Bitcoin Core Has a Fix

Bitcoin Core developers have disclosed three security vulnerabilities in the software that runs most of the Bitcoin network, including one high-severity bug that could disrupt mining, all of which have since been fixed.

Bitcoin Core, the reference software operating the majority of the network’s nodes, classifies vulnerabilities into four tiers, from “low” to “critical,” and these fell into the middle of that range.

The most serious, tracked as CVE-2025-62861, concerns block template creation, the process miners rely on to assemble new blocks.

According to the advisory, a chain reorganization could trigger an erroneous eviction of certain transactions, corrupting a node’s mempool, its waiting room for unconfirmed transactions, so that an affected node could no longer build block templates until it was restarted. For a miner, that means a halt to the very work that earns block rewards.

A second flaw, CVE-2025-62859, could let a peer stall a node’s block processing by announcing a compact block with a manipulated witness, a form of transaction malleation.

None of the three rises to the “critical” level Bitcoin Core reserves for bugs that threaten coin theft at the protocol level, unauthorized coin creation or permanent network-wide chain splits. The developers did not report any evidence the flaws were exploited.

The disclosures come amid a broader reckoning over how quickly Bitcoin’s defenders can keep pace with a shifting threat landscape.

Bitcoin Core recently rewrote its security policy to account for AI, adding a category for “easily discoverable” vulnerabilities that can be surfaced through a simple AI prompt, which it now patches and discloses immediately rather than holding under a long embargo.

That shift reflects mounting concern that large language models have lowered the bar for finding flaws, a worry underscored by the volunteer “Bitcoin Red Team,” which has been racing to uncover AI-discoverable bugs across the ecosystem before attackers can exploit them.

The fixes themselves shipped earlier, with the advisories following under Bitcoin Core’s disclosure timeline. Node operators are generally urged to run the latest software to stay protected.

#4982. What Are Solana Privacy Rings? Inside Helius’ Privacy Protocol for Solana

Every transaction on Solana is public by default. Anyone can look up a wallet address and see its balance, what it has sent and received, and when. That transparency is useful for verifying the network, but a problem for anyone who doesn't want their finances on display: a business paying salaries, a trader building a position, or an individual who simply doesn't want strangers seeing their savings.

Rings are programmable, onchain environments for encrypting money, markets, and finance - without ever leaving Solana

Now live on mainnet. pic.twitter.com/ezCIUCjcbI

Rings support SOL and other tokens on Solana, including SPL and Token-2022 tokens. Users keep custody of their funds throughout, since every transaction needs the owner's signature.

Crucially, the private balances live on the same network as everything else. Private transactions execute directly on Solana and encrypted data is stored on Solana's ledger, with no separate layer-2 network or sequencer in between. That means private balances sit alongside the same stablecoins, tokenized assets and DeFi liquidity as public ones.

Each private transfer comes with a zero-knowledge proof, a piece of cryptography that lets the network confirm the transfer is valid, for example that the sender actually had the funds, without revealing the numbers involved. Rings use a type of zero-knowledge proof called a Groth16 zk-SNARK, which Helius says can be generated in tens of milliseconds, either by a service provider or on the user's own device. Each private transfer settles in a single Solana transaction.

Users read their own encrypted balances with a viewing key. They can decrypt their balance locally, or let a service provider decrypt it and serve it to them, and they can share a key for a single transaction with an auditor or counterparty without exposing the rest of their history.

Moving funds into a Ring from an ordinary public wallet, or back out again, is visible onchain, including the asset and amount. But users who on-ramp from fiat currency straight into a private balance, through a supported provider, keep the asset and amount hidden from the start, according to Helius.

Because Custom Rings interoperate with the default Ring, regulated firms can keep their activity confidential from the market while still sharing the same liquidity as everyone else.

Private transfers are just the start. Solana programs can hold encrypted balances in private escrows and release them when set conditions are met, opening the way for:

At launch, Decrypt, mining and staking app ORE and cross-chain service Aurora Intents were using the default Ring, while Backpack, DFlow, Jupiter, Squads and Titan were among the teams working on integrations.

Helius says the core programs and zero-knowledge circuits have been audited by security firms Certora, OtterSec and ZK Security. Engineers from the Solana Foundation, Blueshift, Zcash and other teams took part in the "trusted setup," the one-off ceremony that generates the parameters the proofs rely on.

The code is open source, published on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, so anyone can inspect how it works.

Formal verification, a mathematical check that the circuits behave exactly as intended, is still underway and expected to finish by the end of 2026. Solana's own documentation currently describes Rings as being in beta.

#4981. FSB urgest Turkey to tighten crypto oversight, set stablecoin rules

The Financial Stability Board cited progress on crypto licensing and urged stronger enforcement and cooperation with foreign regulators.

The Financial Stability Board (FSB) urged Turkey to tighten its oversight of crypto markets and adopt dedicated rules for stablecoins.

In a peer review published on Wednesday, the global financial watchdog said Turkish authorities had made progress by introducing registration and licensing requirements for crypto service providers.

The report was part of the FSB’s regular program of country reviews and assessed Turkey’s progress in implementing the board’s 2023 global recommendations on crypto and stablecoins. It followed a broader 2025 review that found gaps in how jurisdictions had implemented those recommendations.

The FSB recommended that Turkey begin monitoring crypto-related risks to financial stability under a formal framework, strengthen supervision and enforcement, and improve cooperation and information sharing with foreign regulators.

Turkey’s Capital Markets Board introduced licensing and operational requirements for crypto exchanges and custodians in March 2025, including minimum capital thresholds.

The FSB said Turkey had introduced safeguards including requirements to segregate assets held in custody and a ban on domestic crypto payments. The safeguards help limit the spread of crypto-related risks to banks and payment systems. Authorities also launched a centralized platform to monitor crypto activities.

The FSB’s 2025 review found that Turkey had finalized rules for crypto assets but lacked a dedicated stablecoin framework.

In June 2025, Turkey’s Finance Ministry outlined plans to introduce additional transaction checks and limits on stablecoin transfers to combat money laundering.

#4979. Bitcoin Faces First Back-to-Back Annual Losses in History, But There's a Catch

Bitcoin Faces First Back-to-Back Annual Losses in History, But There's a Catch

Bitcoin is flirting with a historical first that bulls probably don’t want to hear: Two consecutive years of losses, something the cryptocurrency has never experienced in its 18-year history.

The world's largest cryptocurrency finished 2025 down 6.34% and has lost another 15.65% so far in 2026, trading around $73,850 on November 10. If Bitcoin fails to recover above its annual opening price of roughly $87,500 before December 31, it will close two calendar years in the red for the first time.

Historical annual returns show Bitcoin has experienced several brutal crashes since its creation, but each negative calendar year has been followed by a positive one. Even the disastrous 2018 and 2022 bear markets failed to produce consecutive annual losses.

The historical pattern is clear. Its significance, however, deserves a closer look.

Bitcoin's previous annual crashes were considerably more painful than its current losing streak. The cryptocurrency plunged 73.56% in 2018 and another 64.27% in 2022, wiping out most of investors' holdings in each respective year.

By comparison, Bitcoin's 6.34% decline in 2025 was relatively mild. Add the roughly 16% loss recorded this year, and the combined decline comes to approximately 21% after accounting for compounding.

That's a fraction of the losses investors endured in previous crypto winters, despite the market potentially recording a longer sequence of negative annual returns.

Bitcoin's performance in 2024 also provides some perspective. The cryptocurrency surged more than 120% that year, meaning investors who bought at the beginning of 2024 would still be sitting on substantial gains despite the subsequent decline.

The picture changes considerably when measuring losses from the market's actual peak instead of calendar-year boundaries.

Bitcoin reached approximately $126,000 in October 2025 before crashing below $58,000 during 2026. That represented a decline exceeding 50%, a significantly more painful move than the 21% combined loss reflected in the two annual candlesticks.

Analysts have pointed to Bitcoin's increasingly institutional investor base, spot exchange-traded funds, and deeper market liquidity as potential explanations for its comparatively smaller bear-market drawdowns.

Those structural changes may help explain why Bitcoin's current market cycle looks different from previous ones, although they have not eliminated major price crashes.

There is also a distinction between the length of a losing streak and the severity of the losses. A market can decline slowly over several calendar years without inflicting the same damage as a single catastrophic year.

And Bitcoin has already demonstrated that a bad year doesn't necessarily translate into a prolonged downturn. The cryptocurrency gained roughly 92% in 2019 following its 2018 collapse and surged more than 155% in 2023 after its disastrous 2022 performance.

For now, Bitcoin has 50 days left in 2026 to avoid its first back-to-back annual losses. A third consecutive decline in 2027 would extend the streak further, but that scenario is still hypothetical.

At its November 10 price of approximately $73,850, Bitcoin would need to gain about 18.5% to recover its 2026 opening price and finish the year in positive territory.

#4978. Bitcoin Covenants Part 5: MATT and OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY — How Bitcoin could carry state across transactions

OP_CCV embeds contract state directly into Taproot output keys and enforces valid state transitions onchain. This makes it possible to achieve stateful contracts and compact fraud proofs.

This is Part 5 in the technical article series about Bitcoin covenants by Cointelegraph Research. To read the previous article click here.

MATT (Merkleize All The Things) is a smart contract framework for Bitcoin that enables stateful contracts and scalable fraud proofs. A stateful contract carries information forward across multiple transactions and can update this information as the contract evolves. Standard Bitcoin scripts do not provide this capability, because each transaction is evaluated independently with no memory of previous executions.

Every covenant proposal allows state-carrying UTXOs to an extent, as illustrated by scripting languages such as Sapio, which builds on OP_CTV. This works by using addresses to represent a finite state automaton, where transactions function as the state transitions. However, there is no way to elegantly implement numerical logic in this paradigm, a gap filled by MATT, and in particular its proposed implementation through OP_CCV. Because MATT allows committed data to be computed at spend time and re-embedded into the next output, each spend can derive a new state dynamically, instead of choosing from a predetermined set of states.

To understand the MATT proposal, it is useful to first review how Taproot commits data through public keys. Every Taproot output contains a base public key, called the internal key, which can be cryptographically modified or “tweaked” to commit to extra information. Formally, the tweaked public key is Q = P + t·G, where P is the internal key, G is the generator of the secp256k1 elliptic curve, and t is a tagged hash of P and the committed data.

In a regular Taproot output, this commitment typically encodes the Merkle root of a taptree, which contains hidden spending paths. MATT builds on this mechanism to also embed contract state into the key. Instead of embedding complex logic directly in Bitcoin’s scripting language, MATT encodes computation as a sequence of state commitments, and the chain verifies only that each state transition is valid.

MATT can be realized through different opcode combinations. The most direct and well-specified implementation relies on OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY (OP_CCV). OP_CCV provides the primitive that makes state-carrying UTXOs feasible within Taproot.  OP_CCV allows a script to verify that a Taproot input or output key has been tweaked to commit to a specific piece of state data. The internal key is first tweaked with a hash of the contract’s current state, and then Taproot’s standard taptree tweak is applied on top. The resulting output key therefore commits to both the tapscript  (the set of spending conditions) and the current state of the contract.

OP_CCV can then enforce what state is carried forward into the next output. It allows the script to inspect the state data provided on the witness stack, perform computations on it, and require that the resulting updated state is correctly re-committed in a specified output. This is how state transitions are enforced on-chain. The stack format is:

OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY

The opcode supports three modes for checking an output as well as a separate input mode. In default mode, the entire BTC value of the input UTXO is allocated to the specified output; in deduct mode, only a portion equal to the output’s amount is assigned, leaving the remainder available for further outputs; and in ignore mode, the script and data commitment are verified without constraining the amount.  Because default and deduct modes are designed to preserve value across checked outputs, transaction fees must be paid through separate fee-paying inputs. A dedicated fee input and change output can be added to the transaction without conflicting with the covenant’s constraints. This prevents the accidental burning of funds that can occur in more primitive covenant implementations, such as OP_CTV or SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT. It also addresses a major limitation of presigned-transaction-style covenants, which typically define amounts upfront and therefore cannot accommodate dynamic fee adjustments or partial unvaults.

When OP_CCV is combined with OP_CAT, the full MATT framework becomes even more expressive. OP_CAT enables byte concatenation in Script, which makes it possible to construct and verify Merkle proofs directly on-chain. Two distinct Merkle trees are associated with a Taproot output in such an arrangement. The first is the familiar Taproot script tree (the taptree), whose leaves are the contract’s spending scripts. The second is a separate state tree, whose leaves are the contract’s data, such as the intermediate steps of a computation.  The OP_CCV + OP_CAT script can verify a Merkle proof against the current state tree root, compute the updated root after a transition, and use OP_CCV to force the next output to commit to it.

This construction enables fraud-proof systems with a slashing condition in which a long computation is committed off-chain, and only the specific disputed step (with its path in the binary tree) needs to be revealed and verified on-chain. Similar systems exist as optimistic rollups on other blockchain systems: the full computation runs off-chain, and the on-chain contract only intervenes when someone raises a challenge. Fraud proofs require that the computation be compiled down to a binary circuit or equivalent step-by-step representation that can be committed to in a Merkle tree. OP_CCV + OP_CAT would avoid the need for the Lamport one-time signatures and pre-signed transaction graphs that BitVM relies on to enforce state consistency.

Beyond fraud proofs, the OP_CCV and OP_CAT combination also has implications for vaults. OP_CCV alone can implement vaults, but when combined with OP_CAT, it allows fully featured vaults that are essentially equivalent to the functionality proposed by OP_VAULT. As James O’Beirne, the author of OP_VAULT, has noted, OP_CCV represents a more general and robust design that effectively supersedes his earlier proposal.

In the next article in this series, we will move on from general covenant proposals to review application-specific opcodes such as OP_VAULT, OP_UNVAULT, and OP_EVICT. Each of the opcodes are designed to solve a specific problem rather than provide broad programmability.

#4977. Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts

Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline.

The collapse of Paraguay’s digital lender Ueno Bank last week left nearly three million customers — roughly 60% of Paraguay’s adults — unable to access their accounts.

Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3 after its solvency ratio fell below half the legally required minimum. An investigation uncovered questionable lending practices and deficiencies in credit documentation and accounting.

The collapse also triggered a political crisis, with thousands taking to the streets to protest and President Santiago Peña attempting to resign before being impeached and arrested on charges of breach of trust and using his office for personal gain.

Paraguay’s peer-to-peer crypto market immediately reflected the turmoil, with some sellers asking for a USDt premium of up to 13%. “USDt is a lifeline for hundreds millions of people in the world,” Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said.

For many, the incident sparked uncertainty over savings, wages and the money needed to cover everyday expenses. With the local guaraní (PYG) currency falling 12.3% in a week, some turned to stablecoins to maintain the value of their funds, or just to keep payments moving along.

David Eisenmann, founder and chief executive of Paraguayan crypto exchange X4T, tells Magazine the timing made the liquidity need even more pronounced.

“The intervention came in the first days of the month,” he says, “exactly when salaries, rent and supplier invoices are due,” adding that many business owners “couldn’t make payroll.” For some, USDt was “suddenly the most liquid money” they had:

But beyond another TradFi masterclass in the virtues of self-custody, Ueno’s collapse highlights the growing role of dollar-pegged stablecoins providing an alternative source of liquidity when traditional banks fail.

Eisenmann says X4T processed more than $10 million in local on-ramp volume over the 30 days to early November, but some of that activity predated Ueno’s collapse.

“The dollar began recovering against the guaraní in October,” he says, “and the Ueno news sped up a move that was already underway.”

Related: Stablecoins can drain from banks and nations at lightning speed

He says the activity “runs in both directions,” with some customers selling crypto for guaraníes or dollars to cover payments they could no longer make through Ueno, while “demand for USDt and USDC as a dollar store of value has risen sharply.”

Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3. Source: Central Bank of Paraguay

As of Nov. 9 the Central Bank said 93.1% of customers with Ueno deposits had been repaid. Despite this confidence has been shaken and X4T continued to see higher online inquiries for dollar-denominated stablecoins. In fact, Eisenmann says the level “has not changed significantly” from the week of the collapse.

Rhys Hicks, associate analyst at data and analytics company GlobalData, says the digital bank’s failure has shown “how much can go wrong when governance does not keep pace with growth.”

That said, he’s not seeing evidence of a mass migration from Paraguayan banks into stablecoins, since other banks “picked up the slack,” and people “seem to have been angrier” with the government than with the banks.

“Some consumers will look for different ways to keep their money safe, but I do not see an overwhelming shift to stablecoins yet,” he says.

Seeking dollars when confidence in domestic banks falters is hardly new. In Argentina’s 2001 financial crisis, the government imposed the “corralito,” restricting cash withdrawals from bank accounts, following a run on deposits.

Related: Peter Thiel backs crypto-friendly Silicon Valley Bank rival — Report

Amid a deepening crisis over the country’s currency peg and sovereign debt, the government later converted dollar-denominated deposits into pesos, reducing people’s savings by about 30% overnight and further damaging confidence in the country’s fraying banking system.

Tether CEO calls USDt a lifeline. Source: Paolo Ardoino

But stablecoins aren’t decentralized and they are not insulated from the banking system either.

During the March 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, stablecoin issuer Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, around 8% of the total, were held at the lender. USDC briefly depegged and fell to 86 cents on secondary markets after Circle said it could not withdraw the funds.

A BIS paper on stablecoins and the international monetary system warns that widespread use of dollar-backed tokens could create challenges for monetary sovereignty in emerging markets.

Hicks says stablecoins can provide an alternative during periods of political instability and “low trust in the local system” because they are pegged to a more stable currency, like the US dollar.

But regulators need to address “transparency” and “consumer protection,” he says, because stablecoin holders don’t benefit from the same deposit guarantees as bank customers, and there is no central bank to step in and make them whole.

Eisenmann says he expects the incident to spark more “diversification,” with people “spreading their money across banks, cash and digital assets” instead of relying on a single institution.

“How quickly trust in the banks returns will depend on how quickly and transparently the authorities handle the resolution,” he says.

#4976. Deutsche Bank Goes Live With Crypto Custody After a Five-Year Buildup

Deutsche Bank Goes Live With Crypto Custody After a Five-Year Buildup

Five years after it first floated the idea, Germany’s largest lender is now holding Bitcoin for clients.

Deutsche Bank said Wednesday that its Digital Asset Custody service has gone live for paying clients, giving institutional and corporate customers in Europe a regulated way to store and transfer Bitcoin, Ethereum and three stablecoins: Circle’s USDC and EURC, plus EURAU.

The bank manages wallets and private keys on clients’ behalf. For now, the service covers custody and transfers, with tokenized financial instruments on its roadmap.

The service is aimed at clients of Deutsche Bank’s corporate and investment banking units, including corporations, asset managers, hedge funds, custodians, brokers and sovereign institutions, according to the bank’s September announcement of the plan.

Its setup includes hardware-based key protection, multi-person approvals and separate warm and cold storage, the bank said.

“In the medium term we aim to deliver a fully integrated, regulated ecosystem that supports the custody, tokenisation, and settlement of digital assets,” said Paul Maley, Deutsche Bank’s global head of trust and securities services.

Deutsche Bank also signed a memorandum of understanding with Deutsche Asset Management, the majority-owned money manager formerly known as DWS, to explore working together on tokenized money market funds, crypto exchange-traded commodities and stablecoins.

The asset manager oversaw about 1.22 trillion euros as of Sept. 30. The bank has also said it plans to expand the custody service to Asia.

The launch caps a long road, going back to at least 2021 when Deutsche Bank began readying a crypto custody and trading platform. Then, in 2023, the bank applied for a digital asset custody license in Germany. Last year, reports said the bank planned to build the service with technology from crypto exchange Bitpanda, alongside its longtime partner Taurus.

Deutsche Bank received authorization from German regulator BaFin under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, or MiCA, which requires crypto service providers to be licensed. The bank cautioned that its custody service doesn’t protect clients against swings in the value of digital assets, fraud or failures by other market participants.

The custody launch isn’t Deutsche Bank’s only crypto bet. The bank is among a group of global lenders, including Goldman Sachs and Citi, backing a $270 million challenge to crypto’s dominant stablecoin issuers.

#4973. This Is How Long Body Recomposition Takes, According to a Physical Therapist

Plus, why it's the fitness goal I recommend to everyone.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a fitness professional and doctor of physical therapy, I’ve always been active. I spent most of my 20s chasing the “toned” look (which, for the record, isn’t even a real thing; it’s marketing jargon). I did all the classic workouts that promised to get me there—high reps, low weights, endless cardio—and prided myself on leaving every class drenched in sweat. I ate as little as possible because I thought that would give me the body I wanted.

Like so many women, I was lean from undereating and overexercising, but I never felt strong—and I definitely didn’t feel good. I had chronic pain, fatigue, and lived on a hamster wheel of more workouts and less food.

Everything changed when I started focusing on building muscle and body recomposition instead. It turns out, what most people mean by “getting toned” is actually body recomp, which, put simply, is losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time.

There’s just one problem. How you get to body recomposition is entirely different from what we’ve been told, especially as women. It’s the ultimate anti–yo-yo goal—and it’s about consistency, not extremes.

I learned how to train for hypertrophy, eat to support recovery, and actually rest—and I got the look (and feel!) I was searching for faster than I expected. Within a year of changing my approach to fitness, I gained eight pounds of muscle and lost roughly five pounds of fat with fewer workouts, more food, no joint pain, and way less effort.

If you’re about to start this journey, here’s how long you can expect it to take.

I’ve successfully recomposed twice and plan to do it again soon, as I’ve just had my second baby.

The first time, I gained eight pounds of muscle and lost five pounds of fat over a year. The second time, postpartum, I gained 4.2 pounds of muscle and lost fat in just a few months.

Muscle tends to come back faster the second time because when you’ve built it once, your muscle fibers retain extra myonuclei (essentially the “brains” of the muscle), which remain even if you lose muscle mass. When you train again, those nuclei help muscle growth happen faster.

That’s why building muscle now is such a valuable investment for your future self.

Body recomposition is a slower process, but that’s exactly why I like it. It forces you to slow down and implement sustainable changes with your training, your nutrition, and your recovery.

It’s tempting to get to your ideal body composition as fast as possible, but rushing it might only make things take longer in the end. For example, overtraining can lead to injury, sidelining you from training, and undereating can prevent muscle growth—or worse, lead to losing it. While this article focuses on the strength training that goes into body recomposition, nutrition and fueling properly are essential because when you’re in too big of a calorie deficit, you can lose both muscle and fat.

Month 1:You might see early fat loss in the first month if you’re in a calorie deficit. Muscle growth typically takes longer, but beginner exercisers might see small developments more quickly than longer-trained individuals.

Month 2:You’ll start to feel stronger as your nervous system adapts and you gain better coordination. You might see muscle definition toward the end of the month because growth can take anywhere from eight to 12 weeks.

Month 3:You’ll likely begin to see visible muscle definition and continued fat loss.

Month 4+:Progress continues, though it’s normal to have slower or plateau phases. Early in training, neuromuscular strength and protein synthesis are more rapid, but as your body becomes accustomed to the stimulus, the improvements can slow. In this phase, it’s important to refine your habits, train close to failure, and find what keeps you consistent.

You can’t rush the process. Building muscle and losing fat simultaneously requires balance—not extremes. If you’re in a 200-to-400-calorie deficit, expect around 0.5 to 1 pound of fat loss per week and visible muscle growth within 8 to 12 weeks, having made good progress toward your goal in three months.

Of course, body recomposition is only possible if you’re focusing on the right things. These are the four most important factors.

Nutrition: Supports Fat Loss And Muscle Growth

I’m not formally trained in nutrition, but here’s what I’ve learned from registered dietitians and what works for me and the Evlo community:

Tracking your food, especially in the beginning, can be incredibly eye-opening. I found I was eating more calories than I realized—and not nearly enough protein. Tracking isn’t for everyone, but it’s a useful tool to build awareness. You can use apps like MyFitnessPal or even list all your food into ChatGPT.

Get started with our Eating for Body Recomp guide

There’s no such thing as a “toning” workout. Fat loss comes primarily from nutrition, not exercise—and you can’t spot-reduce fat. Exercise builds muscle, but only if it’s done with enough mechanical tension and intensity.

Remember: the “burn” you feel during high-rep workouts isn’t what builds muscle. Muscle growth happens from mechanical tension, not just fatigue. That’s why classic “toning” workouts rarely deliver the promise; they’re too light to drive hypertrophy.

Cardio and Activity: Supports Energy Expenditure

Cardio and daily movement are still important, but probably not for the reasons you think.

Although debated in the literature, calories burned from exercise may not be fully additive, especially when in a calorie deficit for recomp. Doing more cardio doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll burn more fat. And, because we want to keep you fresh and not overworked for your strength workouts, I’d say don't overdo it on the cardio. Stay active to keep your energy expenditure high (around 150 minutes of light- to moderate-intensity cardio per week is what I recommend), but don't attempt to "burn off" food, because it likely doesn't work like that anyway and can backfire by negatively influencing your recovery.

That doesn’t mean you should limit activity, since there are plenty of other reasons to do cardio, particularly for your heart. Just don’t rely on cardio alone for fat loss. The biggest driver of body composition change still comes from strength training and nutrition, not from piling on extra miles or minutes.

Recovery: Allows Muscle Growth and Keeps You Consistent

Muscle isn’t built during your workouts, it’s built after them. Recovery allows your muscles to heal, adapt, and grow stronger.

I recommend taking about two days off from lifting each week. Rest days prevent overuse, reduce mental burnout, and help you stay consistent. Mentally reframe your recovery days as productive days in your muscle-building journey.

Not training close enough to failure. Why? It means that you’re not adequately working your muscles—which means you’re not going to get any growth.

Not training close enough to failure happens for several reasons:

How you know you're close to true mechanical failure, not just fatigue:

Failure vs. close to failure: Training to failure means that you cannot do another rep without help. Training close to failure (which is all you need to do) would look like the signs above, meaning you’re 1 to 3 reps away from failure.

I recommend body recomposition as a goal for almost everyone. On the surface, it might sound aesthetic or like another weight-loss strategy, but it’s much more than that. When you build muscle, you’re not just changing how you look; you’re improving your metabolic health, bone density, longevity, and even your mental health.

And, for the record: body recomposition can happen even without weight loss. When muscle increases and fat decreases, your body composition improves, even if the number on the scale doesn’t change.

Pure weight loss actually often causes muscle loss along with fat. That’s because calorie deficits drive weight loss, but when calories drop too low, you end up losing both fat and muscle.

Recomposition takes time, precision, and experimentation. You’ll need to find the right calorie level (which may take some experimenting), balance your training, and stay consistent long enough to see results. But if you commit to this process over the course of a year, you’ll not only improve your body composition, but also build skills and awareness you can use for the rest of your life.

Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is the founder and CEO of Evlo Fitness, a science-based program designed to build muscle with less wear-and-tear on the body. As a doctor of physical therapy with over 15 years of experience, she saw firsthand how high-intensity workouts led to chronic pain, fatigue, and hormonal imbalances in women. Determined to shift the fitness paradigm, she created Evlo — a program led exclusively by Doctors of Physical Therapy, emphasizing strength training through Gentle Consistency™.

Through Evlo and her podcast, The Doctor Shannon Show (4.9 stars, Spotify & Apple, 200+ episodes), Dr. Shannon educates women on the science of exercise, debunking fitness myths and promoting sustainable health. Originally from Kansas, she now lives in Austin, Texas, with her husband and two children.

#4972. Tether's Tiny AI Agent Beats Models 2.5 Times Its Size at Controlling Your Phone

Tether's Tiny AI Agent Beats Models 2.5 Times Its Size at Controlling Your Phone

Tether, the company behind the world's largest stablecoin, USDT, is getting surprisingly good at making tiny AI models punch above their weight.

The company on Wednesday unveiled QVAC BotPsy, an 800-million-parameter AI agent designed to carry out everyday tasks on personal devices. Parameters are essentially the knobs that determine how much an AI model can do, and more of them generally translate to improved performance. And for reference, frontier AI models today run in the trillions of parameters.

In the company's own testing, Tether’s relatively tiny model outperformed competitors with up to 2.5 times as many parameters, suggesting that AI assistants may not need enormous models to get things done.

Unlike traditional chatbots that simply respond to questions, BotPsy is agentic, meaning it’s designed to take action. It can identify which tools an application needs, execute commands in the right order, and adjust when something goes wrong.

For example, Tether described a benchmark scenario in which an AI assistant needed to send a message but encountered two problems: Wi-Fi was disabled and the inbox was full. BotPsy turned on Wi-Fi, cleared enough storage, and completed the task, while the underlying model repeatedly attempted the same failed operation.

That's a fairly mundane achievement, but it's precisely the kind of problem that makes AI agents useful outside a chatbot window.

BotPsy is built on Alibaba's Qwen3.5-0.8B architecture, a relatively small language model that Tether trained further to specialize in interacting with software tools. Its 800 million parameters represent the numerical values the model learned during training, and a smaller parameter count generally means less memory is needed to run it.

According to Tether's technical documentation, BotPsy scored 44.0% on BFCL v4, a benchmark that evaluates an AI system's ability to select and execute software functions across different tasks and conversations. Scores reflect a weighted percentage of successful performance across tool-use categories.

The underlying Qwen3.5-0.8B model scored 23.4%, while the considerably larger Qwen3.5-2B reached 37.7%.

BotPsy also scored 58.7% on ACEBench, which evaluates the accuracy of function calls, including selecting the appropriate tools and arguments. Its base model managed 30.1%, while the 2-billion-parameter competitor scored 55.4%.

The company tested five models across six tool-use evaluations, with BotPsy posting the highest results on five. Its average score across those tests reached 45.0%, compared with 38.8% for the larger Qwen model.

BotPsy is the latest addition to QVAC, Tether's effort to build an AI ecosystem that runs on devices controlled by users rather than relying entirely on centralized cloud infrastructure.

The company first introduced QVAC in May 2025, positioning the project as an alternative to AI services operated by technology giants. Its longer-term ambitions included autonomous agents capable of interacting with applications and potentially making payments using Bitcoin and USDT.

Tether expanded that initiative in October 2025 with a 41-billion-token dataset for training science and engineering models, alongside QVAC Workbench, an application that lets users run AI models locally.

Earlier this year, Tether released its SDK, providing developers with tools to build offline AI applications across mobile and desktop operating systems.

The company also developed QVAC MedPsy, a medical AI system designed to run on consumer hardware. Its 1.7-billion-parameter version outperformed Google's much larger MedGemma-27B on HealthBench Hard, a test of realistic clinical conversations evaluated using physician-developed criteria.

BotPsy is currently available as an open-weight model under the Apache 2.0 license, meaning developers can download, modify, and integrate it into their own applications. Tether has also released compressed versions intended to reduce memory requirements for local deployment.

The company has not announced a release date for a finished consumer assistant powered by BotPsy. Its published model card also says the training code and training data are not included in the release.

#4970. Want to Get Closer With Your Spouse? Take on a Wife Carrying Competition.

One couple‘s experience taking on a race that demands they shoulder each others’ burdens—literally.

DANNY AND KATIE Young are both active, but they’re not exactly the type of couple that stakes out dates on their calendar for the next Hyrox doubles race. Over the last few years, however, both went through separate fitness journeys. So on Christmas Day 2025 when Danny's older brother, Dylan, asked if they had heard of a wild event called wife carrying, they felt ready to take on a new challenge together.

Danny and Katie watched YouTube clips of the North American Wife Carrying Championship, an annual race held every October at the Sunday River Resort in Newry, Maine. It’s exactly what the name implies: a 278-yard race where husbands carry their wives on their backs. This is not the only one of its kind—similar events are staged around the globe and there’s a world championship in Finland—and competition isn’t limited to only married or man-woman couples. The Youngs scrolled through videos of couples running a steep obstacle course, jumping hurdles and sloshing through mud pits all while struggling to stay upright to the finish. The Youngs decided they wanted to take on the event in the coming year.

“One, because it’s so silly and ridiculous,” Katie tells Men’s Health. “Two, we used to live in Boston and we wanted to get back up to New England. The competition (held October 10 this year) was right around our 16th wedding anniversary, so we figured, what better way to celebrate?”

“We are seize the moment people–even if the moment is 10 months in advance,” Danny adds. “Signing up for the competition also felt like a natural celebratory culmination of what we’d done in the last year. We felt like: this is just the sort of thing we’ve been getting ready for. Let’s go do that, to applaud a really cool year of physical and health transformation.”

DANNY AND KATIE met when they were 14 years old, dated in high school, and got married shortly after graduating college. Now 38, they live on a hobby homestead outside of Asheville, NC. Their day jobs (Danny works as a manager at Trader Joe’s, Katie is a clinical supervisor for a community mental health clinic) and taking care of their daughter, Opal, and their small farm leaves little time for traditional training.

But Katie and Danny have navigated the challenges that come with maintaining fitness through both the busy schedules of everyday life and unexpected circumstances. In August of 2023, Katie had ankle surgery and was non-weight bearing for 14 weeks. She gained more than 100 pounds, which was difficult to manage on her 5’3’’ frame. By Thanksgiving of 2023, she started walking with a crutch, but she wasn’t able to return to her workouts (mostly hot yoga) until the summer of 2024. She loves power flows, hot HIIT classes, and hot lifts. “If it’s not over 100 degrees, I’m not interested,” Katie says. “I like that it’s balance, strength, and there’s a cardio element at times.” Twice a week turned to four times a week and then six; by the summer of 2026, she had lost 120 pounds.

Danny had been a CrossFit devotee in his 20s. His job at Trader Joe’s is very physical, picking up and carrying 20 to 50 pound boxes throughout the day. He had abandoned his gym habit in his late 20s; by 30, he struggled with back problems. He returned to the gym three years ago, alternating between calisthenics and foundational compound lifts. He trained twice a week, then three times, then every day. He, too, spent the last year transforming his body from a “dad bod” to one chiseled with muscles—and in top shape, stands at 6’3” and weighs 185 pounds.

But in June of this year, Danny injured his back during a deadlift session. He didn’t lift any weights for the rest of the summer. The couple were still committed to take on the wife carrying contest—but they needed to find a new way to train. They leaned on their active lifestyle on the homestead. They keep four goats, and Katie found that carrying two five-gallon buckets of water up and down the farm’s hills several times a week increased her strength. Katie often picked up one of the 80-pound goats to “escort her out of my garden, where she wants to eat my pumpkins.”

When Danny carried the buckets, he’d sometimes throw Katie on his back. He also carried her around the house and up and down the hills near the farm. They discussed which carry style might work best for them, trying piggyback, upside-down, and other methods. They never attempted a full 278-yard training run, instead opting for spontaneous moments of carrying when circumstances allowed.

“I really like the dual challenge of it, which appeals to both of us,” Danny says. “It’s like a test of a relationship alongside a physical feat. Silly, physical antics are part of our love language.”

RACE MORNING IN Newry, Maine brought clear, blue skies and strong winds. Almost five dozen couples warmed up by jogging up and down the rolling hills of the Sunday River Ski Resort ski slope, navigating sections of the 278-yard course and attempting the log hurdle in the carry position. That’s one of the two dry obstacles on the course; the other is a sand trap.

Danny and Katie watched other couples warming up and did some light stretching. Danny pumped out several sets of pushups as they waited. Hundreds of spectators lined the course.

“The community element seemed really fun,” Katie says afterward. “I can see why a lot of people watch it every year, or why people participate every year.” They met a couple who’d traveled from Utah to compete. Another pair had participated every year for the last 25, while others were in their 60s.

An M.C. announced each set of couples, who competed against one another in rounds of two and for time; the fastest two teams from the qualifying rounds would compete head-to-head in a final heat to determine the winner. A record 58 couples had signed up to compete.

Finally, it was their turn. Katie and Danny wished good luck to their co-competitors, and after several false starts as the MC adjusted his mic, the couples took off. Danny jogged as Katie held on to him utilizing a variation of the popular “Estonian carry,” where she was positioned upside-down, facing his back, using her arms to grip her own legs, which were wrapped over his shoulders like a yolk. The strength and balance she’d built through yoga showed as she held steady, despite Danny’s wobbles on the uneven terrain. She relied on core strength primarily, but also her arms and inner thighs to stay in position.

“It turns out that holding on to your own legs like an upside down human backpack while your partner runs uphill, clambers over a log hurdle, and wades through mud is much harder than it looks,” Katie says. “You’ve got to crunch up as tight as you can, squeeze your legs around your partner, wrap your arms into your own legs, and brace your core; all the while feeling your blood rushing to your head. I think the only reason I was able to do it is from the strength, endurance, and flexibility I’ve gained from my hot yoga practice. Plus, if you can tolerate exercising in a 105 degree room, what’s a little bit of mud?”

The pair didn’t talk much during the race itself. “Most of the race, the noise I was making was something along the lines of, ‘this is so much harder than I thought it was gonna be,’” Danny recalls.

Katie felt the early section had gone well, even though she admittedly couldn’t see anything but the landscape passing below her. “And then, all of a sudden, I can see the ground is moving a lot slower, and Danny's panting and saying how hard it is,” she says.

Still, they kept moving, navigating a steep uphill and then descending toward the mud pit, the course’s final challenge also known as the “Widow-Maker.” Katie had photographed the mud pit prior to the race and texted her friends with the caption, “My fate.”

Danny stepped into the mud hole, navigating the first big step downward. He wobbled. Katie, sensing his unsteadiness, didn’t want to be dropped on her neck and head. “So I abandoned ship,” she says. She threw herself into the cold, wet mud, which filled her mouth and covered her eyes and nose. “It was a pretty solid belly flop,” she added. The muddy water coated her body, officially making the Youngs the first full “mud drop” out of the 30-plus couples that had competed up to that point.

“As I felt her coming off of my back, I thought, ‘where is she going?’” Danny adds afterward.

Katie stood up, wet and laughing so hard she needed a moment to steady herself. The plan had been for Katie to carry Danny across the finish line–but after they cleared the mud pit and stepped onto dry land, he was so wet and she was laughing so hard, she couldn't quite grip him. She jumped onto him, piggy-back, as they emerged from the mud pit and jogged the final yards to the finish line. Just before crossing, she hopped off his back and picked him up, carrying Danny across the finish, laughing as the crowd cheered.

The winning couple was celebrating their 10th anniversary, and their children joined them in crossing the finish line. Most of the competitors stayed through the full two-hour event, as did the spectators, watching the award ceremony and cheering for the various additional contests (best dressed couple and other superlatives.) The winning couple received the wife's weight in beer and five times her weight in cash. Volunteers handed out beers to the entrants. Katie changed out of her wet clothes before they joined his parents, Dylan and his wife, Kristen, and Katie and Danny’s 8-year-old daughter, Opal.

In carrying Danny across the finish, Katie wanted to reinforce what Opal had learned: “Mommy and Daddy are both strong and capable, and there’s no difference,” Katie says.

OVERALL, THE BIGGEST takeaway from the race had little to do with their time or the physical challenge that came with hauling one another across the course. Their relationship, they say, has always been strong—and attempting a fun, unique competition reinforced the tenets of their partnership: fun, laughter, strength, and supporting each other.

Danny suggested they enter again next year, “which I’m definitely up for, competition-wise,” Katie says. “I want to do many ridiculous competitions with you,” Danny adds. “Our relationship quality has been great, and this added another fun adventure.”

After the race, Danny considered how he might approach training for their next attempt. “If we were to run it back, I would definitely add hill sprints to my routine,” he says. “I should have prepared for the fact that the race is very short and very intense. Interval sprints and sled pushing would have been more aligned with the demands of the competition.”

But nothing, in his opinion, is better than replicating the real challenge of the event: carrying a partner and working together. “Spend as much time as possible with your wife on your back,” he says. “It's kooky and fun, and there's nothing else that quite mimics the awkwardness of two spouses becoming one athlete.”

#4969. Deutsche Bank launches crypto custody for companies and institutions

Clients can store and transfer Bitcoin, Ether and select stablecoins through the bank, which manages their wallets and private keys.

Germany’s largest lender, Deutsche Bank, launched its crypto custody service for institutional and corporate clients on Wednesday, according to an announcement shared with Cointelegraph.

The bank also signed a memorandum of understanding with Deutsche Asset Management, its majority-owned asset manager, to explore collaboration on tokenized money market funds, crypto asset exchange-traded commodities and stablecoins.

Deutsche Bank announced plans to offer the service to institutional and corporate clients in Europe on Sept. 16, pending regulatory clearance. Deutsche Bank’s listing for crypto custody and transfer services in the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) register is dated Oct. 12 and names Germany’s BaFin as its regulator.

The service initially supports Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and select stablecoins, including Circle’s USDC (USDC) and EURC (EURC), as well as AllUnity EURAU.

Gerald Podobnik, co-head of Deutsche Bank’s corporate bank, told Reuters in October that the bank planned to launch in Germany before expanding to Asian financial centers in 2027.

Deutsche Bank partnered with crypto infrastructure provider Taurus in 2023 to develop custody services after applying for a digital asset custody license in Germany.

#4966. This New AI Music Model Is Already Better Than Suno—We Put ACE to the Test

This New AI Music Model Is Already Better Than Suno—We Put ACE to the Test

Artificial intelligence has gotten pretty good at writing songs. Now, a relatively unfamiliar competitor has managed to beat Suno, arguably the biggest name in AI music, at its own game.

ACE Music v1, developed by ACE Studio, has taken first place on Artificial Analysis' vocal music leaderboard, scoring 1,160 Elo points against Suno v6's 1,144.

The AA-Music-Vocal v1.1 benchmark measures the quality of AI-generated songs containing vocals. Evaluators listen to tracks produced from identical prompts without knowing which model created them, then choose their favorite. Those preferences determine an Elo-style rating, with higher scores indicating stronger listener preference.

The lead is relatively narrow, and the models' statistical confidence intervals overlap. Suno also retains the top position on the separate instrumental music leaderboard.

ACE Studio, founded in 2018, originally focused on synthesizing singing voices from MIDI notes and lyrics. Its latest ACE Music v1 model generates complete songs from written descriptions or user-provided lyrics.

In Decrypt's hands-on tests, ACE Music consistently produced more melodic and coherent songs in mainstream styles.

That said, the vocal performances sounded more natural in general, with fewer of the synthetic artifacts that sometimes make AI singers sound like they're struggling to pronounce their own lyrics, use a lot of autotune or hallucinate words just to fill spaces. (Go ahead and give our song a listen here, which incidentally is about our latest company announcement regarding the Information Exchange.)

ACE also handled song endings better. Where Suno occasionally introduces strange sounds, unnecessary repetitions, hallucinations or abrupt musical changes near the finish, ACE generally maintained its structure and delivered cleaner conclusions.

That matters because making a convincing chorus is relatively easy compared with maintaining a musical idea throughout an entire composition even if the lyrics are already over.

Suno still had an advantage when we pushed the models toward less conventional genres.

In our melodic death metal test, ACE consistently produced tracks featuring a woman singing clearly in a pleasant, clean voice, missing the aggressive vocal delivery expected from the requested style. In general it confuses metal genres all over. Suno offered more creative arrangements in the proper heavy styles, with better stylistic consistency in several similarly demanding prompts.

The results were subjective rather than a controlled benchmark, but they showed why a leaderboard victory doesn't automatically make one model better for every musician.

ACE's most interesting feature may be its songwriting workflow.

Its “Idea” feature can develop a basic concept into lyrics and a structured composition, identifying individual song sections and describing how they should be arranged. Users can then refine the material rather than repeatedly generating completely new tracks.

The v1.1 Preview goes further, creating a musical score before generating audio.

“Each generation is a new performance, so the sound may differ even when the score stays the same,” the developers explain.

Users can edit melodies and chords, regenerate performances, export MIDI files and separate vocals from instruments for further production.

That workflow puts ACE closer to a music production assistant than a simple prompt-to-song application.

The flagship ACE Music v1 model remains closed-source with no public API, so users can only generate via the official site. However, its developers are pursuing a parallel open-source strategy.

ACE Studio and StepFun have already released ACE-Step 1.5, a separate family of models whose code and weights are publicly available. Unlike the proprietary flagship, these can run on users' own hardware—but using a weaker model.

The company also promises another release.

“We plan to open-source ACE Music v1 Flash in late 2026,” the developers state on their website, describing a version designed to balance quality, generation speed and hardware requirements.

ACE Music is available through its browser application, with a limited free tier and paid subscriptions. Commercial usage rights for flagship-model songs require a paid plan, while ACE-Step offers a separate free generation option.

For now, ACE Music v1 holds a 16-point Elo lead over Suno v6 in vocal generation. Its promised Flash release would give local users another model to try before the end of 2026.

#4963. Do You Need a Vitamin B12 Supplement If You’re Taking a GLP-1?

Here’s why you don’t want vitamin B12 levels getting too low.

WHILE GLP-1 MEDS have been game changers for weight management, they’ve also introduced some challenges for people looking to lose weight. They reduce appetite and help you feel satisfied sooner, but that can make it more challenging to get all the nutrients your body needs.

One of the nutrients GLP-1 users may get less of is Vitamin B12. On social media, people discussing life on GLP-1s often bring up eating more foods high in B12 or recommending B12 supplements when complaints of side effects like fatigue and headaches come up.

Here’s what you need to know about vitamin B12 and GLP-1s along with how to make sure you’re getting enough.

VITAMIN B12, ALSO known as cobalamin, is an essential vitamin that cannot be produced by the body. It must come from food or supplements, says internist Jennifer Chung, MD.

Vitamin B12 supports several important bodily functions. It’s involved in the production of red blood cells, creation of DNA, and maintenance of a healthy nervous system. The demand for vitamin B12—the recommended daily intake of vitamin B12 for most adults is 2.4 micrograms—doesn’t go away even when you’re consuming fewer calories.

WHEN VITAMIN B12 levels drop too low, the effects can range from fatigue and weakness to more serious symptoms. Dr. Chung says this might involve anemia, which is a lack of healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout the body, tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, and problems with balance or memory. If vitamin B12 deficiency persists, you may run the risk of permanent nerve damage.

TAKING A GLP-1 doesn’t automatically mean you’ll develop a B12 deficiency. It’s more of an indirect effect.

“GLP-1 medications are not known to reduce absorption of vitamin B12, unlike metformin, which interferes with the binding of vitamin B12 in the gastrointestinal tract,” explains Dr. Chung. “Instead, nutrient deficiencies with GLP-1 medications arise from a combination of eating less food, eating less dietary variety, delayed gastric emptying, and rapid weight loss.”

The common side effects people experience while taking a GLP-1—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation—may also contribute to not getting enough vitamins like B12.

DOCTORS SAY A vitamin B12 supplement is worth considering for GLP-1 users, but it’s not a requirement.

“Several medical societies recommend that GLP-1 users consider supplementation with vitamin D, calcium, B12, and a multivitamin to reduce micronutrient deficiencies, but there is no universal recommendation,” says Dr. Chung.

Todd Worley, MD, bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist at Houston Methodist Willowbrook Hospital, says the primary goal is to get enough of this essential nutrient through food.

B12 is found in a variety of animal-based foods, including beef, poultry, salmon, tuna, trout, eggs, clams, and dairy products. You can also find a comprehensive list of B12-rich foods here.

If a reduced appetite is making you unable to stomach enough food, then it’s time to consider a supplement. Another reason to consider a supplement is if you follow a plant-based or vegan diet.

Jacqueline Vernarelli, PhD, nutrition scientist at Sacred Heart University, says that unfortified plant foods aren’t a reliable source of the nutrient since vitamin B12 is primarily in animal-based foods. As a result, she recommends regularly incorporating B12-fortified foods, such as certain breakfast cereals and plant-based milks, to help meet your daily intake.

AGE AND SOME gastrointestinal conditions can also make it harder for your body to absorb the vitamin. “Conditions that reduce stomach acid increase with age, and stomach acid is needed to release vitamin B12 from protein in food so it can be absorbed,” says Dr. Chung. Guys might start feeling the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency in their 50s.

A B12 DEFICIENCY can be difficult to recognize because symptoms often develop gradually and may overlap with other issues. For example, you may attribute fatigue to not eating enough overall when it’s actually because you’re low on B12.

Dr. Chung recommends talking with the physician who prescribed your GLP-1 about any changes you’re feeling. They may recommend blood tests to check your B12 levels.

If blood tests confirm a B12 deficiency, your doctor may recommend dietary changes or a supplement.

Oral B12 supplements in capsule, tablet, or liquid form are often the first line of defense, with a common daily dose of 1,000 micrograms, says Dr. Chung. The reason supplements have larger doses than the recommended daily intake is because the body only absorbs a portion of the vitamin. Intramuscular B12 injections are also an option, but Dr. Worley says those are usually reserved for folks with absorption problems or more significant B12 deficiencies.

The right dose and form of B12 supplementation will depend on your individual needs. There’s no one-size-fits-all approach. Above all, Dr. Chung recommends being proactive and planning meals with enough B12 sources and keeping tabs on any signs of potential deficiencies. Losing weight shouldn’t mean sacrificing good health.

#4961. Bitcoin hovers near $74K as stocks rise despite US bond yield rebound

Bitcoin traded in a narrow range as investors bought the dip in tech stocks and US bond yields climbed on high CPI inflation data.

Bitcoin (BTC) circled $74,000 at Wednesday’s Wall Street open as stock markets rallied and US bond yields surged.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD diverging from US equities as investors resumed buying the dip in tech stocks.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The AI sector led the day’s early gains, with cloud-computing company CoreWeave jumping over 20% after reporting better-than-expected Q3 revenue and lifting its 2026 guidance.

CoreWeave stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Nvidia, which suffered on Monday and Tuesday amid ongoing controversy over CEO Jensen Huang, opened around 2.5% higher.

Nvidia stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Oil prices, meanwhile, gained on the day amid fading optimism over a diplomatic solution to the US-Iran war. As attacks on ships traversing the Strait of Hormuz continued, analysis pointed to several practical hurdles to restoring pre-conflict traffic levels, even if a deal is reached.

“Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase in flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk,” LSEG Oil Research wrote in a note on Tuesday, according to Reuters.

US WTI crude oil was up 1.4% on the day at $87.70 per barrel after dropping to $84 on Tuesday, its lowest since late August. Brent crude gained 1.5% to $93.40.

Stocks rose even after Tuesday’s higher-than-expected Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation data pushed US bond yields sharply higher. The 10-year yield returned to 5% on Wednesday for the first time since Oct. 29, while the 30-year yield reached as high as 5.378%, a level last seen on Oct. 22.

US 10-year bond yield one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, said that bonds were pricing in a more hawkish approach to interest rates by the US Federal Reserve. Markets have priced in a 0.25% rate hike in December, with the odds of a 0.5% move now increasing.

“Inflation breakevens today are focused on the drop in oil prices while regular Treasuries today are reacting to a Fed that is definitely going to hike next month, as of now, with one another in January,” Boockvar told CNBC.

Related: Here’s what happened in crypto today

Bitcoin continued to trade in a narrow range between its 21-week and 50-week simple moving average at $73,078 and $75,492, respectively. Volatility cooled as traders awaited a new catalyst after the CPI report.

BTC/USD one-day chart with 21-week and 50-week SMAs. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Investor profitability suffered as Bitcoin lost support around $75,700, the aggregate cost basis of the short-term holder (STH) cohort - entities holding a given amount of BTC without selling for up to 155 days.

On Tuesday, STH wallets sent over 47,000 BTC to exchanges at an unrealized loss, potentially signaling an increase in panic selling if those coins were sold.

#4959. OKXICE moves ahead with tokenized stocks as blue chips push back

The Nov. 23 debut puts a new SEC exemption to the test as Nasdaq pursues its own tokenized stock plans after warning that trading across platforms could fragment liquidity.

Crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) are set to launch tokenized stock trading on Nov. 23, despite objections from 67 companies to having their shares listed and warnings from Nasdaq that trading across disconnected platforms could fragment liquidity.

The venture, known as OKXICE, will operate under the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s temporary Innovation Exemption and offer eligible US customers round-the-clock trading. Under the exemption, venues must give companies a chance to object before listing shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. JPMorgan Chase, McDonald’s, SpaceX and Coca-Cola were among the companies that objected.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens that represent company shares or track their price. The rights they carry depend on how they are structured. The distributed value of tokenized stocks and ETFs reached $3.88 billion on Nov. 11, up 13.4% over 30 days.

In comments to Cointelegraph, former New York governor and OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo said investors would have “the same rights, protections and ownership that come with the underlying shares.”

OKX expects the venue to list more than 70 assets, including 59 exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and tokenized shares of Coinbase, Circle, BitGo, Robinhood and Strategy. The lineup also includes Strategy’s preferred shares.

Related: Public companies object to OKX-ICE’s tokenized stock plan

The rollout comes amid concerns that trading the same shares across traditional exchanges and blockchain platforms could split liquidity and make prices less reliable.

In October, a study by the International Monetary Fund found that the tokenized stocks were about 1.5 times as volatile as the same stocks in traditional markets. Decentralized exchanges had the weakest liquidity and their prices strayed further from those in traditional markets than prices on centralized exchanges did.

The IMF also warned that combining trading and settlement on a blockchain could remove safeguards that help markets absorb shocks. As tokenized markets grow, greater use of leverage and closer links between markets could amplify fire sales, liquidity runs and financial contagion.

Nasdaq argued in a January filing that trading tokenized stocks on platforms outside traditional rails could fragment liquidity and make it harder for investors to get the best available price. Regular US stock trading runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern time on weekdays, excluding market holidays, though some brokers offer premarket, after-hours and overnight trading.

Cuomo described the current market structure was “built for another era,” arguing that crypto markets had already shown that trading could run around the clock. “Now we are bringing that standard to equities, without asking investors to settle for synthetic exposure or give up their shareholder rights,” he said.
