#4926. In This Midcentury Nashville Home a Mosaic Rainbow-Hued Window Brings Color to the Earthy Interiors

Here’s one you may not have heard before: What do Serge Mouille sconces, a Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant, and Borge Mogensen dining chairs have in common? Hint, hint: They all live in the Nashville home of Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of antiques and vintage furniture store Eneby Home.

One might reasonably presume the home of antiques purveyors to be chock-full of one-of-a-kind finds from far-flung locales, and while that is certainly the case here, the husband-and-wife duo’s house otherwise expertly subverts expectations.

Built in 1970, the uber-quiet four-acre property sits at the top of a hill overlooking seemingly endless rolling valleys. It’s surrounded by native honeysuckle bushes and Tennessee Fieldstone, and the sun sets on the front side of the home at 6:37 p.m., says Doug, who dreamed of building what he describes as an “art gallery” for their furniture.

The Jenkinses kept the wall of original Tennessee Fieldstone—and the original copper fireplace—but added their own flair with vintage furnishings, like a La Mura sofa, Gianfranco Frattini for Cassina leather lounge chairs, a Charles Dudouyt credenza, and a 1960s marble fossil coffee table from Italy. “It’s super unique,” says Doug. “It doesn’t have a name behind it.”

Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of Eneby Home, with their daughters. They kept the original Tennessee Fieldstone on the wall and paired it with an antique marble dining table that’s “huge and heavy,” says Doug. “The guys hated bringing stuff to our house.” Even though the Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant is often seen in copper, the Jenkins were able to source one with a green finish, seen here. The chairs are Borge Mogensen; the 1960s geometric painting is from France.

A well-lit workspace features a vintage 1950s desk, an Italian cocoon lamp, and a Hans Wegner chair from Denmark.

“There’s not a lot of this type of house in Nashville,” says Greg Dutton, the founder and architect behind Columbus, Ohio-based and AD PRO Directory design firm Dutton Studio. “But we had to look past what was there—a mixed bag with a new era in each room—to create a backdrop for the work they do.”

Cue the blank slate. The couple bought the house as-is—black toilets, mustard-hued siding, and early 2000s kitchen included—and embarked on a “bigger than expected” renovation, says Doug, that translated to moving walls, updating floor plans, a new roof and flooring, and overall furnishings, of course.

With the resulting minimalist white walls and clean lines, how does one amass the amount of character evident here? “When you build in materials that have inherent imperfection, that naturally bakes in a lot of warmth,” says Dutton. Think locally sourced, character-grade white oak flooring throughout; imported reclaimed European bluestone that’s well over 100 years old in the primary bath; and an original copper fireplace in the living room.

“The mosaic supposedly came from a building in Bologna,” says Doug. “The morning sun comes up on this side” and ignites a fire of filtered light within the home.

“The island has a commercial look to it,” says Doug of the Vipp system. “It hit every box. It’s sick.” Dutton helped reconfigure the space’s floor plan to open the room to the dining area. The oven is by Miele.

A Guillerme et Chambron cabinet, sourced from Eneby Home, houses curiosities. The 1960s pendant light is Stilnovo.

The guest bathroom originally had a black toilet and smoked glass. Now it features vintage Serge Mouille sconces, of which Doug has “never seen another pair,” a 250-year-old antique Italian mirror from the 1800s, and a Josef Hoffman bench.

“Flaws make the house feel better, not worse,” says Dutton. “But creating something that looks effortless actually takes a lot of coordination. We wanted it to feel like it had just happened that way, and installing materials that feel like they’ve been there forever automatically gives the house permanence and ensures it’ll age gracefully over time.”

The push-and-pull between old and new, simple and full of character, clean and distressed is one the Jenkins family is familiar with. The balancing act makes the house interesting, says Doug, and the same inclination to lean on historic materials translates just as well to furnishings.

“Some of this stuff we’d been saving in hopes we’d one day be able to use it for our own house,” says Doug. One such example is a 1940s or ’50s-era, rainbow-hued mosaic window the couple bought five years ago and stored in a crate ever since. “We asked Greg to change the layout of the wall to make it work,” says Doug. The stone sculpture on display in front of the window is another; it’s 2,000 years old, from Rome.

An earthy palette in the primary bedroom lets the landscape through the windows do the talking. The sconces are by Biny; the oversized 1880 landscape painting is from France; the chairs are Borge Mogensen; the side table is Charles Dudouyt, and the floor lamp is La Borne.

“The fireplace is original, and we ran with it,” says Doug. “It’s New Mexico style and is super cool.” It’s paired with an abstract geometric art piece and a collection of vases from Denmark.

The stainless steel Vipp island in the kitchen, which the couple found in Denmark, is “the best thing in the house,” says Carina. “We moved from a house with a big pantry, and it was a challenge to figure out where everything would go. This island holds a lot.” Here, the family embraces the “European model” of compact living–albeit in 4,500 square feet. Dutton designed the black cabinetry wall as a backdrop for the island, which he calls a “piece of jewelry.”

Like any gallerist worth his salt, Doug spends five minutes each night turning off all of the ambient lighting in the house, like a pair of midcentury Biny sconces in the primary bedroom, an Orocolo lamp in the living room, and a 1970s Marika Carniti Bollea Nautilus lamp in the kitchen. Much of the light shines on a collection of artwork that’s so vast it’s often swapped out.

“We’ve already traded a few things,” says Doug. “If we find something we love, we want to use it. It’s what we do. It’s a perk, for sure.”

As is a home that’s forever. “Our girls want to come here when we’re old with their own kids,” says Carina. “They love it so much.”

The 1950s painting is from Denmark, the 1970s vase is from Sweden, the 1970s stool is Pierre Chapo, and the ceramic is from France. “We spend a lot of time in Denmark and like to mix Danish and Swedish,” says Doug. “We know a lot about that style of furniture.”

Dutton reworked the floor plan in the primary bathroom to set the vanity under a skylight. “We don’t use much overhead lighting,” says Carina.

#4924. This Popular Supplement May Also Be the Key Behind Healthier Knees

You’re probably not getting enough of it, either.

Knee osteoarthritis can be a debilitating condition due to the joint pain, stiffness, and swelling it causes. Unfortunately, it's a reality for an estimated 14 million Americans. There are a range of potential treatment options that can help, including cortisone shots and GLP-1s, but a new study suggests a more accessible option may also help: taking a fiber supplement.

Research from a recent clinical trial published in the journal Nutrients suggests that adding a daily fiber supplement could ease pain from knee osteoarthritis, strengthen your muscles, and maybe even make you feel pain less intensely.

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends having 14 grams of fiber for every 1,000 calories you consume, which means most women should aim for 25 grams of fiber daily, while men should strive for 38 grams each day. But the average American only eats around 17 grams of fiber per day, suggesting that many of us consistently fall short on this important nutrient.

Experts aren’t saying that you should take a fiber supplement instead of physical therapy or seeing a specialist for knee pain. But if you're doing everything else right, adding a fiber supplement to your routine might be worth trying out. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher in the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham; Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology; Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California

For the study, researchers recruited 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis and split them into four groups. One group took a 20-gram daily inulin supplement (inulin is a naturally occurring fiber that's considered a prebiotic—it’s also commonly found in healthier soda alternatives), another did digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE), the third group did a combination of inulin and physical therapy, and the final group took a placebo.

Researchers discovered that people in the inulin and PT groups had less knee pain, and that people who took inulin had other perks that didn't surface in the physical therapy group, like better grip strength and less pain sensitivity. Also worth noting: Those who took inulin were more likely to stick with their prescribed treatment compared to the 21 percent of people in the PT-only group who dropped out.

“Earlier studies had linked certain gut bacteria, such as Streptococcus, to worse knee pain,” says Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher at the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham. That, plus feedback from people suffering from knee arthritis who said they wanted diet-based ways to manage their pain, led Kouraki and her team to study inulin.

The researchers didn't study the why behind this association, but experts have a few theories. "Good gut bacteria feed on fiber like inulin and, in doing so, they produce substances that calm inflammation and help keep the gut lining healthy," Kouraki says. Your gut "talks" to your brain and nerves, and it can influence how sensitive you are to pain, she explains.

Kouraki points out that people in the study who took inulin also had higher levels of the gut hormone GLP-1 (yep, that GLP-1), which is also tied to pain regulation, and that those with bigger rises in GLP-1 tended to have a stronger grip. "These clues are early, and we need more research to understand exactly what’s going on," she says.

But it's important to put the findings into context. "Exercise still did more to improve walking and chair-rise ability, which matters for patients," says Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

And while the findings suggested perks with taking an inulin supplement, they weren't huge differences, points out Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology. "At best, further study is warranted," he says.

People concerned about their joints will often take collagen, glucosamine and/or chondroitin. But "there is no strong evidence to support the use of dietary supplements," Dr. Harvey says.

Kouraki also points out that collagen and glucosamine are aimed at the joint itself, while inulin works indirectly through the gut bacteria and the body’s immune and hormone systems. "It’s a different approach, using diet and the gut to help manage symptoms,” she says.

Knee pain is complicated, and it's a stretch to say that taking a fiber supplement will make everything better. "This doesn’t replace proven treatments like exercise and physiotherapy, which also worked well in our study," Kouraki says. "But it suggests diet could be a useful extra tool."

If you're struggling with knee pain, Dr. Gibson recommends doing the following:

And, of course, if you're in pain and it's not getting better, talk to your doctor. They should be able to suggest alternative strategies to make you more comfortable.

#4922. Suiet wallet to shut down in latest exit from Sui ecosystem

The self-custodial wallet will keep its API services running through Nov. 14. Sui’s DeFi total value locked has fallen more than 22% over the past month.

Cryptocurrency wallet Suiet is shutting down, adding to a series of closures and service withdrawals in the Sui ecosystem.

Suiet, a self-custodial wallet built for the Sui blockchain, said in a notice that it will stop updating and supporting its wallet, with API services set to end after Nov. 14. The shutdown comes as the Sui network has seen a sharp decline in decentralized finance (DeFi) activity.

Sui’s total value locked (TVL) stood at about $413 million on Wednesday, down more than 22% over the past month, according to DefiLlama data. Data from Token Terminal shows that Sui averaged about 128,000 daily active users in October, down from 601,000 in November 2025 – or around a 79% drop.

Meanwhile, other recent closures have also raised concerns about the costs and challenges of keeping projects running on the Sui network.

“Sui’s problems seem to mostly be of an economic nature resulting from expensive engineering costs and low user volume rather than protocol failures,” Kadan Stadelmann, former chief technology officer of Komodo Platform, told Cointelegraph. “No flaw in the system’s core design has been found.”

Cointelegraph reached out to the Sui Foundation and Suiet for comment but had not received responses by publication.

Related: Sui DeFi protocol Full Sail to wind down after Switchboard incident

Suiet’s shutdown immediately follows the Sui-based hardware wallet project Suiball also announcing its closure on Nov. 10. Meanwhile wallet provider Phantom ended support for Sui in September.

DeFi project Full Sail also shut down following a security incident involving Switchboard that caused about $91,000 in losses.

Despite the decline in active users, transactions on Sui have increased, reaching 324 million in October, up from 101 million in November 2025, according to Token Terminal. However, more transactions do not necessarily mean more users, and wallet providers must still decide whether supporting the network is worth the cost, according to Stadelmann.

“Multi-chain wallets have expansive attack surfaces, and Sui’s approach adds costs for vendors who can take their business to less capital intensive chains,” he said. “Any individual failure of a multi-chain wallet is more a reflection of the risks rather than an indictment of any given protocol.”

Sui has also experienced four network outages in 2026, resulting in around 22 hours of combined downtime, according to reports published by the Sui Foundation.

The network stopped processing transactions for about six hours in January, followed by three more outages on May 28 and 29. The May disruptions were linked to software bugs, including problems introduced by a network update, the Sui Foundation said at the time.

By comparison, rival blockchain Solana has not recorded a network-wide outage since February 2024, when it went offline for nearly five hours. Meanwhile, Aptos, which uses the same underlying smart contract programming language as Sui, last reported a mainnet outage in October 2023.

Network outages are significant because they can prevent DeFi users from trading, transferring funds or managing positions, although the Sui Foundation said no user funds were at risk during its May disruptions.

#4921. Not Ready For a Facelift? No Problem: Welcome to The Era of “In-Between” Treatments.

No surgery, minimal downtime, a firmer, more lifted look—what’s not to love?

THE RISE OF BUZZY noninvasive in-office treatments is no coincidence. These days, people want to look sculpted, lifted, and more refreshed without having to make the somewhat uneasy decision to go under the knife. And as more and more patients seek meaningful results without committing to surgery, there’s a growing interest in treatments that bridge the gap between injectables and a facelift, aptly dubbed the “in-between” treatments.

These interventions will still give you meaningful lifting, volumizing, sculpting, and tightening results without as much downtime (sometimes, none at all) or diminishing returns on your investment. Think of them as the individualized, targeted treatments you can utilize before considering a face or neck lift. The trick is having a solid understanding of what specific technologies can—and cannot—accomplish. If you’re not pairing the right treatment with the right concern, you’re shelling out good money to “correct something it fundamentally cannot address,” explains Connie Yang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City.

Filler, for instance, is effective for restoring strategic areas of volume loss on the face, but it can’t truly lift tissue or remove excess skin. “If you add more filler in an attempt to recreate a sharper jawline or lift the lower face, you’re just going to end up making the face look heavier and puffier, rather than more lifted and sculpted,” says Dr. Yang.

Meet the experts: Connie Yang, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. Jennifer Levine, MD, is a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon in New York City.

In a similar vein to filler, energy-based skin devices such as radio frequency (think: Morpheus 8 or Xerf) or ultrasound devices such as Ultherapy that target the deeper, structural layers of the face can only do so much up to a certain point. “These treatments can give meaningful improvement in the right patient, but there’s a limit to how much contraction you can achieve non-surgically,” says Dr. Yang. If someone has significant jowling, excess skin, or deeper tissue descent, repeated treatment with these types of devices will end up giving someone only progressively smaller improvements over time.

To give you the LD on all of your options, we spoke with experts about what each treatment can realistically accomplish, what patients can expect over time results-wise, and when you should skip straight to surgery.

As a rule of thumb, most (not all) aesthetic professionals will generally advise you to exhaust all options before spending a pretty penny on a facelift. In the end, it’s an individual decision. Either way, in-office treatments can help to keep your skin radiant and build collagen to help you to get an even better result for when it is time for a facelift. Think about throwing a crumpled up sheet over your mattress in the morning: If you don’t iron it first, the wrinkles will still be there when you go to make the bed.

There's no one-size-fits-all approach because not all facial aging is the same. For patients that are truly getting closer to being surgical candidates, “focusing on improving skin quality and some degree of skin tightening can be your best bet, while at the same time managing expectations of the limitations of devices and their expected outcomes,” says Dr. Yang.

Double board-certified facial plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine, MD, who uses a combination of injectable treatments and non-surgical devices in addition to surgery in her practice, recommends treatment protocols depending on which components of aging are most responsible for the patient’s concerns.

The following treatment categories are considered the in-betweeners that you may want to consider before going under the knife.

“This is an important option for select patients with earlier skin laxity who want gradual tightening and a degree of lifting,” says Dr. Levine. Ultrasound imaging allows providers to actually visualize tissue layers and guide energy placement.

It’s FDA-cleared for use to lift the brows and help with lax tissue beneath the chin and neck—the places where aging skin can be most obvious. “I consider it an in-between treatment because it can address laxity through targeted tissue remodeling while the patient’s expectations remain appropriate for a nonsurgical result,” says Dr. Yang, but “[they do] not replicate the degree of lifting you can achieve surgically.”

These work best when texture, dermal remodeling, and modest tightening are the goals. Dr. Levine says that for these treatments, energy settings and treatment depth play a huge role and must be chosen carefully based on anatomy. RF microneedling is provider-dependent, especially because at the wrong setting, facial fat loss, unintended scarring, and nerve injury can occur.

“I consider this particularly valuable when fine lines, uneven pigmentation, and textural changes contribute substantially to an aged appearance,” explains Dr. Levine. Improving the skin’s surface can make a meaningful aesthetic difference, especially for someone who is beginning to develop skin laxity. She points out that “improvement in skin quality is a different endpoint from repositioning descended facial tissue.”

Ellacor is the best example of a true in-between option, says Dr. Yang, “because it actually removes microscopic cores of skin without surgery, allowing the skin to contract as it heals.” Instead of just heating the skin to stimulate collagen, it uses tiny hollow needles to physically remove microscopic columns of excess skin, scarlessly. As the skin heals, it contracts and remodels, which can help to improve wrinkles and laxity.

Patient selection for this treatment is especially important because there is some downtime involved and a risk of pigment change. That said, it’s useful for those with mild to moderate laxity and early jowling, who don’t quite have enough excess skin or tissue to warrant a facelift yet.

Brand Names: Sculptra, Radiesse, Juvederm, Restylane

When true volume deficiency contributes to someone’s overall concern, Dr. Levine says that conservative volume restoration with the use of hyaluronic acid fillers or biostimulatory injectables that boost skin’s own collagen production can help to improve contours and balance the face.

Let’s just get this out of the way right off the bat—age alone isn’t the biggest determining factor in whether or not someone would benefit from a facelift. Genetics, lifestyle choices, and how someone cares for their body and skin have a huge impact. “I have patients in their 40s with very little laxity who are excellent candidates for non-invasive treatments and younger patients whose anatomy or degree of tissue descent make certain treatments less effective,” explains Yang.

And while there’s no single telltale sign to know when it’s time for a facelift, one of the main factors is whether the patient has “skin laxity alone or true tissue descent that requires surgical repositioning,” says Dr. Yang. With skin laxity, the skin can appear creepy or loose with decreased elasticity and can be pinched more easily. “Tissue descent is a deeper structural change; if you manually reposition the deeper tissue upward and it significantly restores the contours of the cheek or jawline, that tells me that the concern isn’t just loose skin and that a facelift would be the solution,” explains Dr. Yang.

Even if someone is a candidate for a non-invasive treatment, if they're ultimately looking for a dramatic lift or significant change in their facial contours, then surgery may be the answer. Dr. Yang says that she is more inclined to recommend surgery after a patient has gone through multiple rounds of injectables or tightening treatments and they continue to chase the same concern with diminishing improvement or returns. “At that point, continuing to add filler or repeatedly treating with devices can become costly without addressing the underlying structural issue,” she says.

Before diving face first into a surgery, Dr. Yang encourages her own patients to really explore all of their options and think deeply about their long-term goals. If you know that a facelift is in your future, it may shape what is recommended to you by a provider. “I don’t want you spending years of over-treating or investing in procedures that may only give you marginal improvement.” Instead, she says, the focus should be on maintaining skin quality and aging well until you’re ready. Conversely, if you’re unsure whether surgery will ever be an option for you, finding the right provider to work with can help you to maximize non-surgical options available in order to get the most meaningful results possible.

Overall, the goal should be to maximize what you have and age well, while recognizing when you’ve reached the limitations of non-surgical treatments. “If surgery may eventually be the right choice, you want to arrive there with healthy, well-maintained skin,” she says. Amen to that.

#4919. Victorian Architecture Meets Mediterranean Charm in This Warm and Whimsical London Home

Interior designer Marta de la Rica describes herself as “a New Yorker by birth, French by adoption, and Spanish at heart.” That mix of cultures would prove to be an asset for one of her recent projects: the 5,382-square-foot four-story home of a family of four in London. A fine example of Victorian architecture, the building, located in the quiet residential neighborhood of Battersea and only steps away from Battersea Park, was built in 1879. “I already knew the clients, since I had previously designed their home in Bilbao, and I knew what kind of atmosphere the family wanted as well as what was particularly important to them about their home,” says de la Rica.

The walls of the stairwell are painted in Yel-01 Smooth by Clayworks and the Clam Shell Large light fixtures are by Porta Romana. The floor is made of several different marbles: Negro Marquina, Perlado, and Rojo Alicante.

The young family is originally from Spain but had already been living in London for nearly 10 years when they decided to buy a single-family home there. De la Rica decided to design spaces for them with a British-Mediterranean look that reflects the character of the historic Victorian architecture and the demands of modern family life. “The family wanted an elegant and peaceful home that, above all, would be warm and cozy,” says de la Rica. “For us, that meant creating spaces with comfort, character, and personality.”

Two midcentury armchairs sit in front of a Louis XIV fireplace from 1700.

Light brown and rust tones dominate the living room’s color palette.

Since the clients are Spanish, the project had a particularly interesting cultural dimension for the designer, as she explains: “We wanted the house to feel personal to them while also remaining true to its London identity and the Victorian architecture. So the project became a dialogue between English interior design and a more relaxed, Mediterranean lifestyle,” says de la Rica.

De la Rica’s interiors combine English interior design and a relaxed lifestyle in this Victorian building where the sunroom doubles as a dining room.

Originally, the family had been looking for a home in a different part of London, but when they saw this house, they were immediately taken with it and changed their plans. The building’s structure was in very good condition; only the floor plan needed to be reconfigured. “Above all, we wanted to preserve the spacious rooms, the ceiling heights, the bay windows, and the staircase,” explains the designer.

A relaxed breakfast setting with chairs by Vintola Studio and Benjamin pendant lights from Felix Lighting,

Visually, all the rooms have an almost opulent feel, yet at the same time, each one reflects its particular purpose. The ground floor includes a study, a living room, a kitchen, af amily room, and a sunroom, which also serves as the dining room. The parents’ bedroom is located on the second floor. A separate children’s area with bedrooms and play areas was created on the top floor. “The sunroom is a big part of the character of the house. To build the basement, it had to be demolished and rebuilt. It was very important to us to preserve the extraordinary presence of this space and its connection to the rest of the house,” says de la Rica.

The designer made the transitions from one room to the next as natural as possible by ensuring that the materials and atmosphere flow seamlessly.

The living spaces flow into the garden (designed by Matthew Wilson) and the terraces in front of the family room and the sunroom provide direct access to the outdoors. The garden features a pool, an outdoor kitchen, and a spacious dining area, providing additional spaces for social gatherings. The interior is characterized by elegant craftsmanship, custom details, warm colors, and high-quality materials. These choices highlight the grandeur of the historic home while also creating a cozy atmosphere.

A 20th-century dresser serves as a nightstand in the primary bedroom; an onyx lamp sits next to a vase filled with flowers.

“I particularly like that the rooms all have their own character, yet there is a clear, unifying design that carries throughout the house,” says the designer. It was also important to de la Rica to emphasize the scale of the house without having it feel cold or ostentatious. “Even in the larger rooms, there’s a coziness. It was very important to us to achieve this balance,” she says.

In the guest bathroom, the walls are painted in Yel-01 Smooth by Clayworks. Below the Negro Marquina marble sink by MDLR-Design, a curtain of Marly fabric by Colony.

The playroom showcases the Victorian architecture.

The children’s rooms are located under the mansard roof, which is typical of many Victorian houses in London. For the two youngest members of the family, the designer transformed the entire top floor with its sloped ceilings into colorful playrooms.

Amid dinosaurs and Mickey Mouse toys, the family’s son sleeps here. A Globe ceiling light hangs above the bed (Olofane).

De la Rica’s favorite parts of the house, however, are the living room and the dining room. For her, these are the areas where the home truly comes to life and where the design directly interacts with the family’s daily routine.

Above the large sofa in the family room, a Soren globe light from Pinch. The cream-colored Mayan Cuzco rug is from Bellbridge.

She particularly likes that the living room, dining room, and kitchen form a single, open space. “This part of the house allows for a very uncomplicated way of living,” she explains. “It’s very beautiful but not contrived or overly formal. It exudes coziness and spontaneity, and for me, that’s ultimately what makes a family home.”

For the walls in this bathroom, the designer chose Oli-03 Smooth by Clayworks, wall sconces by Vaughan, and a Calacatta Viola marble sink.

The wardrobe in the guest bedroom is upholstered with Ticking Stripe 1 Black fabric (Ian Mankin). The decorative Flax 03 tassels are from Samuel & Sons.

In the daughter’s bedroom, the rug is from Kvadrat. The closet doors are upholstered with fabrics from Yutes.

The Bert & May tiles in Garnet and Sand White were custom-made for this bathroom. The bathtub is Perlado marble.

#4918. MSCI confirms Strategy’s removal from indexes at end of November

Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi are marked for deletion in MSCI’s final list, with changes taking effect after the Nov. 30 close.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses.

MSCI’s final list of affected securities, released as part of its November index review, lists “STRATEGY A” with the action “Deleted.” Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist.

The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30, under the implementation timetable MSCI announced in October.

Removal could prompt funds tracking the affected benchmarks to sell the companies’ shares, reducing a source of passive investment demand.

As Cointelegraph reported in October, JPMorgan previously estimated that Strategy’s exclusion could trigger roughly $2.8 billion in selling.

Strategy opposed the proposal, arguing that it repackaged MSCI’s earlier effort to exclude digital asset treasury companies and injected policy judgments into index construction.

The company nevertheless played down the potential disruption. In its consultation response, Strategy said MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding and less than one day’s trading volume.

#4917. 7 Best Wrinkle Creams of 2026, Tested by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

Our picks span everything from luxe, high-tech finds to drugstore gems.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Since celebrating a milestone birthday (yay!), I've started to notice a few fine lines and wrinkles that weren't on my face the previous year (ugh!).

Now look, there's nothing wrong with aging gracefully—it's a celebration of a life well-lived—but I'd be lying to your face if I didn't admit that these changes caught me off guard and made me reevaluate my skincare routine. I've tried a few red light therapy devices, and they're helpful—but they're also incredibly pricey. And I'm super-uncomfortable around needles, so injectables like Botox and hyaluronic acid fillers are out of the question—at least for now. The doctors I consulted told me there is no quick fix for aging, but wrinkle creams are a pain-free and surprisingly affordable way to plump unwanted lines. (Our recommendations start at just $22.)

A great wrinkle cream helps hydrate and plump the skin, which ultimately makes fine lines and wrinkles less obvious, so you'll want to start in your 20s when collagen (that's the protein that plumps skin) production slows down. "Prevention is always the best strategy, so consider using a wrinkle cream before wrinkles are especially noticeable," says dermatologist Geeta Yadav, MD. "If you can already see a wrinkle form when you make facial expressions, it may be a good time to integrate a wrinkle cream into your regimen."

Sounds pretty sweet, no? Well, the pros say we'll need to be patient when using wrinkle creams, but the results—and you will see results from the right cream—are worth the wait. You should notice an immediate hydration boost, but wrinkles won't visibly begin to diminish until you've been consistently using your new cream anywhere from 6 to 12 weeks, according to dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD.

Retinol is the holy grail of anti-aging ingredients since it helps stimulate collagen production which results in a plumper, more youthful appearance. SkinMedica has this dermatologist-approved ingredient in spades and unlike other wrinkle creams, you can pick from multiple retinol strengths: 0.25 for beginners, while 0.5 and 1.0 are for the most advanced anti-aging benefits. "Once your skin fully adjusts to retinol, you'll want to try more potent concentrations so you continue to see results," suggests Dr. Yadav.

Beyond retinol, this wrinkle cream is also formulated with SkinMedica's PhytoShield Complex, a proprietary formula of antioxidants that improve skin texture and minimize irritation. To help combat any inflammation your skin may experience, the wrinkle cream's formula also includes magnolia bark extract.

"SkinMedica is a brand I've trusted for years, and their retinol product is, in my opinion, the gold-standard on the market," says Underwood. "I love that it comes in multiple strengths, so you can customize the treatment strength, whether you're a retinol newbie or a seasoned user, like myself."

Underwood says that the formula itself is pretty creamy and moisturizing—a major plus for these types of products—making it a solid choice for normal to dry skin. You'll still need to layer a serum or moisturizer underneath for extra hydration and to prevent potential redness, flaking, and sensitivity. Once your skin becomes used to the low retinol concentration, you can eventually skip the extra step.

"I noticed results from consistent use after about six weeks—and I've been using this product off and on for years," Underwood says. "My horizontal lines have definitely been softened and my skin is glowy and refined. This is worth every cent."

Also, our biggest tip with using this wrinkle cream is to begin twice weekly to avoid any potential flaking or redness typically associated with retinol use, then graduate to nightly use. Apply in the evening after cleansing and toning and before applying your moisturizer.

If you aren't looking to break the bank on a wrinkle cream, Neutrogena's Rapid Repair wrinkle cream is a solid choice, Dr. Yadav says. "I like this product from Neutrogena because it’s a concentrated, yet gentle formula that is also easy to find and has an accessible price point."

In addition to fighting fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots using retinol (found in many pricier alternatives), the cream is also formulated with hyaluronic acid to hydrate skin, which plumps it up and smoothes the look of lines. Typically, retinol is used at nighttime to avoid irritation, but Neutrogena actually advises using this wrinkle cream twice daily. I was a bit nervous about these instructions, but since my skin is used to retinol and I liberally reapply broad-spectrum sunscreen, I decided to give it a shot.

After slathering on a pearl-sized amount to my freshly cleansed face and neck, I noticed my skin looked more radiant after a few days. With regular use, my smile lines and even some acne-related dark spots also looked less obvious. It also contains similar ingredients to pricer wrinkle creams, including Skinmedica, Dr. Dennis Gross, and Lancôme, but at a fraction of the cost.

One thing to keep in mind is that it isn’t the most cosmetically elegant. Don’t get me wrong. Neutrogena performs well, especially for the price, but I found the cream pills more frequently on my skin than pricier options. That said, as long as I regularly use a face exfoliant then the pilling is relatively minimal.

Caring for sensitive skin can be a real drag since redness, itching, stinging, peeling, and dryness can commonly occur. Thankfully, dermatologist Dr. Dennis Gross, MD, created a sensitive skin-friendly wrinkle cream that's safe for retinol beginners.

How? It's infused with Phyto-Retinol Blend that combines retinol with bakuchiol, rambutan, and ferulic acid to help minimize the retinol uglies that would normally leave skin red and itchy. "That means you get a powerful cocktail of line-minimizing ingredients with pretty much no irritation—a huge plus in my book," says Underwood, who loves this moisturizer because it absorbs into his skin beautifully, leaving it hydrated and plump.

Given Underwood's glowing review and my general love of other Dr. Dennis Gross products, I gave this wrinkle cream a shot. It's a soft, semi-thick cream that spreads across my skin like butter on warm toast. My face is definitely glowing whenever I apply this face cream.

Since I frequently test new beauty products, my skin has become quite reactive. But, I haven't experienced any irritation on my skin since incorporating this epic face cream into my routine. After just two weeks of twice daily use, I noticed my smile lines and hyperpigmentation began to disappear. These spots are normally very stubborn and can take months to vanish, so I was pretty surprised to see speedy results.

That said, you probably won't love this face cream if you're already using a prescription-strength retinoid, like tretinoin, because your skin is used to a quicker exfoliation process. This wrinkle cream combines a super gentle retinol and a plant-based alternative, while prescriptions work much faster but with the risk of irritation. Still, my retinoid–related redness and dryness have practically disappeared since using this soothing face cream, making it a must-have in my routine. I'll continue reaching for this moisturizer when I don’t apply my prescription retinoid cream so my face can still enjoy the hydrating and light brightening effect in the summer without the flakes or itching.

If you're looking for a tried-and-true performer, you've found it here. "Retinol is the most effective over-the-counter wrinkle fighter and RoC is a pioneer in the use of this ingredient," Underwood says. He likes this night treatment because it's a great non-irritating option that's also infused with glycolic acid to minimize the appearance of dark spots.With regular use, you'll notice a more radiant complexion, and deep wrinkles will begin to smooth. It'll take about 12 weeks of daily use before you (and those lucky enough to be around you) will notice visible results. And don't worry about over-exfoliation: RoC contains glycerin and dimethicone for instant skin hydration.

It is important, though, to limit your usage of this product to nighttime only, just as it says on the instructions (you're a rule follower, right?). Because it contains both retinol and glycolic acid—two powerful active ingredients that refine skin texture—this could make your skin extra sun-sensitive if you use it during the day. Sunburns? No thank you. So be sure to slather on your go-to face sunscreen, such as my all-time favorite one from Isdin that helps reverse sun damage.

Olay's Regenerist moisturizer is made with one of the smoothest and creamiest formulas on the list—I love massaging it on. The best part? Hyaluronic acid gives my face instant hydration, which is a welcome year-round treat.

Shea butter is a superstar moisturizer that is like a refreshing glass of water for dry skin and helps maintain dewiness. The antioxidant-rich ingredient helps calm irritation and is even safe for someone with nut allergies because it’s made entirely of fat, according to Cleveland Clinic. Niacinamide, also known as vitamin B-3, helps boost skin cell turnover so skin is extra firm and glowy. Also in there: antioxidants to help fend off the free radical damage caused by air pollution, sun exposure, and smoke that can lead to weaker collagen and cause wrinkles. Free radicals can also cause redness, dryness, and eczema, Dr. Dennis Gross previously told WH.

For me, the rich texture is a winner because it's completely non-greasy, making this formula ideal for dry skin, and surprisingly suitable for my oily skin. Since it's on the thicker side, it'll take a few minutes for my skin to fully absorb the cream, but I don't mind because my face looks and feels noticeably softer. I knew this cream was really working when my friends started asking what I've been using on my face—and swapping in this Olay cream was the only significant change I'd made.

Underwood agrees: "Who says you have to pay a lot for an effective wrinkle cream? Not me," he says. "Olay's classic 'red jar' cream is packed with decades of anti-aging skin science."

The greasy feel of certain skincare products can be unpleasant, but that certainly isn't Lancôme's anti-aging cream. "I often find fancy wrinkle creams to be overly fragranced and far too thick," Underwood says. "That's not the case with this cream, which has a lighter, almost whipped texture that hydrates beautifully without a hint of greasiness."

Like Underwood, I found this wrinkle cream to have a whipped-like texture, and in my experience, it provides ample hydration without congesting my pores. As for the anti-aging benefits, in the short-term I've experienced a more even-toned complexion and my fine lines are less noticeable.

In the long-term Rénergie can help with lower face sagging by using a blend of potent ingredients. "It's a trifecta of active ingredients—moisturizing hyaluronic acid, line-smoothing peptides, and skin-evening niacinamide—handily tackles visible signs of aging with regular use," Underwood says. He recommends making it the last step in your nighttime routine to help prevent moisture loss.

The only downside with this moisturizer is the price. However, the quality of anti-aging superstar ingredients coupled with display-worthy packaging helps justify the added cost. And FWIW, this is the only refillable option on this list. For example, a 1.7-ounce jar of Lancôme’s face cream costs $150, while a same-size refill will only set you back $130. Since each jar is estimated to last two months, you’ll save $100 a year just by purchasing the refills.

"While not typically found in wrinkle creams, daily sun protection is crucial to prevent further wrinkles and skin damage,” says dermatologist Marie Jhin, MD. Since sunscreen is a non-negotiable part of a proper anti-aging skincare routine, Dr. Jhin appreciates the combo of broad-spectrum SPF 30 coverage with hydrating hyaluronic acid and ceramides to keep your skin moisturized and protected.

This CeraVe day cream is also made with encapsulated retinol, a type of non-irritating retinol, to further smooth uneven texture and improve the look of fine lines. The ceramides also help with wrinkle prevention, since they help restore the skin's barrier.

I gotta be completely honest, I didn't love this day cream because it leaves behind a white cast on my complexion, and for that reason alone, it's an automatic return for me. (For reference, I wear shade 9 in Armani Luminous Silk Foundation.) However, if you have a lighter complexion than I do, you should be fine. Here's what I do like: The thicker texture spreads surprisingly well across my face and doesn't pill when layered under my face makeup. It also doesn't make my normally oily skin look like a greasy slice of pizza. Instead, it adds more of a natural-looking luminous glow which is appreciated in the summer.

Also, keep in mind you should apply this wrinkle cream at least 15 minutes before sun exposure and then every two hours for adequate sun protection. So as long as you have the time commitment and a white cast isn't a typical problem you've dealt with, then you're probs a good fit for this wrinkle cream.

The pros I chatted with say the two most important factors to look out for when buying wrinkle creams are your skin type and the active ingredients in the formula. Here are some shopping pointers.

First, you must pair your wrinkle cream with sun protection—up to 90% of visible skin aging is from the sun. "UV exposure from the sun speeds up the aging process by breaking down collagen and elastin, and it can cause pigmentation (such as sun spots and melasma)," says dermatologist Nazanin Saedi, MD.

Retinoids are a class of vitamin A derivatives (like the OTC version, retinol) that are "the single most proven anti-aging ingredients, after sun protection," says dermatologist Hadley King, MD. They boost cell turnover, collagen and elastin, and minimize discoloration, says Dr. King. It's also a fantastic ingredient for treating adult acne and those with oily skin.

Here's the catch: You'll need to start off using a pea-sized amount to avoid irritation, and pregnant women can't use it, says Dr. Spearman. You can also use the sandwich method, which involves adding a base layer of moisturizer, adding the retinol on top, and following up with another layer of moisturizer. Thankfully, there are some very effective retinol alternatives such as plant-based bakuchiol which do a lot of the same great things as retinol, but are safe for pregnant women or those with very sensitive skin, says Dr. Spearman.

Using these proven ingredients isn't enough. "Just as on food labels, ingredients are listed in order of their amounts," says Dr. King. Your safest bet is to use wrinkle creams with the active ingredients listed earlier on in the label instead of at the end for the most effective, anti-aging results. While the order of ingredients does give some information, it's not really enough to know the concentrations unless these are also listed—some brands that pride themselves on transparency do this, but most don't, says Dr. King.

Our skin type also informs our ideal wrinkle cream. For example, those with oily, acne-prone, or combination skin will appreciate a lightweight wrinkle cream, while those with dry skin should look for a richer formula that offers ample hydration. "Heavier creams tend to work better for more mature, more dehydrated skin,” says Dr. Spearman. “These are often too much for those who are acne prone or have oily areas of skin." Generally, brands will list on the box which skin type will benefit from using its creams.

Our team has written about wrinkle creams since September 2023. With endless options on the market (and I mean hundreds!), it can be hard to narrow down what the best options for your skin are. So to help, I chatted with several dermatologists and Women's Health's beauty director Brian Underwood to curate a list of wrinkle creams you'll love adding to your skincare routine.

To ensure we only feature the latest and most effective launches in November 2026, I tested a bunch of wrinkle creams to deliver my unfiltered testing experience to help you determine which one is most ideal for your needs. I carefully researched wrinkle creams aligned with the above expert guidance. As a quick reminder this includes the best ingredients and skin types they’re compatible with. I also considered pricing, each cream’s consistency, how fast they absorb, and the short- and long-term benefits they offer. Additionally, I evaluated how well they layered with other products, like sunscreen and foundation—and nixed anything that pilled.

Ultimately, I tested dozens and settled on the featured picks that earned major snaps from me, my fellow WH editors, and the doctors I consulted.

There are many processes that the body goes through when aging, and one of those is the production of less collagen, which can make your skin more susceptible to wrinkles, Dr. Yadav says. Collagen is what helps the skin maintain its elasticity and resilience.

As you age, cellular turnover also decreases, which causes dead skin cells to build up on the surface of the skin, making its texture look rougher and uneven, and exacerbating the appearance of wrinkles, Dr. Yadav says.

When you opt for wrinkle creams that fight these two things, they can promote stronger, firmer, smoother, and more even-looking skin, Dr. Yadav says. "Additionally, adding moisture into the skin helps to plump up the look of fine lines, albeit temporarily," she adds.

There's really no specific age that's best for working a wrinkle cream into your skincare routine, since people can form wrinkles at different ages depending on their lifestyle, sun exposure, and heredity, Dr. Yadav says.

On the other hand, Dr. Jhin suggests people can start using a wrinkle cream as early as their 20s. "Even though many people start using anti-aging products in their 40s or 50s when signs of aging have become more prominent, your skin’s natural collagen production actually starts to decline around age 25," she says.

Dr. Jhin often tells her patients to think of skincare as a marathon—not a sprint. "There is no 'quick fix' for aging," Dr. Jhin says. "Like regular exercise and a well-rounded diet help you maintain a healthy body, continued, regular use of anti-aging products will help your appearance in the long run."

#4914. Inside the Underground Mosques of Kazakhstan’s Surreal Mangystau Desert

Up until about 20 years ago, a faint trail up a steep hill through limestone-and-chalk cliffs was the only way to reach Beket-Ata, one of the sacred underground mosques—as they’re colloquially known—of Kazakhstan’s Mangystau desert. “There was no proper path then, but people made the difficult climb in the heat and wind,” my guide, Yerzhan Nagmanov, tells me as we embark on our way to the holy site—eased slightly by the stairs now carved into the stone. That arduous journey, the travelers believed, “was part of the pilgrimage.”

En route to Beket-Ata with Mangystau Tour 999, visitors walk a trail cutting through the steep hill.

The trail of stairs descending into the canyon en route to Beket-Ata.

As inhospitable as the roughly 64,000-square-mile desert may seem, it has attracted scores of people over the years arriving to see Beket-Ata and the four other sacred complexes scattered across its expanse: Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe. Traveling between the five holy sites, the distinction between architecture and geology evaporates into the desert heat: Walls, ceilings, and floors are all variations of the rock from which the mosques were excavated. For pilgrims, the journey to these sacred sites is an act of devotion, where people come to honor revered Sufi masters, pray for blessings, and seek spiritual guidance in times of difficulty.

The mosques are hundreds of years old, collectively dating between the 12th and 18th centuries, but they’re new to the UNESCO World Heritage List as of this summer. The “Rock Mosques and Associated Sacred Sites of Mangystau” were added to the esteemed collection of landmarks in July.

Each mosque is associated with a different spiritual master within Sufism, the mystical branch of Islam. The five Sufi masters’ influence shaped the region’s religious landscape, and then the landscape itself, as all of the mosques—crafted in a rock-cut style that grew out of nomadic building traditions—seem to grow directly from the desert terrain; they’re carved into caves, tucked along the contours of cliffs and hillsides, and tunneled below the ground.

After three weeks travelling through Kazakhstan’s cities, mountains, and pine forests, I spent my final week in Mangystau, a landscape so different from anything I’d seen so far in the country that it felt like a whole world unto itself. Having recently visited Astana’s Grand Mosque, with its blue domes, soaring minarets, and gleaming expanses of marble, I wondered whether Mangystau’s rock-cut shrines might fall flat by comparison. For me, however, their lack of splashy grandeur is precisely what made them so compelling.

A stately arch welcomes travelers to the steps leading to Beket-Ata.

While I am not Muslim, I was fascinated by how the Sufi masters traversed this unforgiving terrain along with their families. Some walked hundreds of kilometers to establish places of worship far from the comforts of the world, spending years in prayer and contemplation before eventually being buried here. I was drawn to the way the rock mosques embody a humble yet stunning expression of faith shaped by the austere landscape, where instead of gilded shrines or massive palaces, devotion found a more organic form. Through guided 4x4 tours with Red Maya Travel and Mangystau Tour 999, I visited all five.

A necropolis inside the Shopan-Ata complex.

My first stop on the tour is Shopan-Ata, named after the 12th-century Sufi teacher. The complex consists of a vast necropolis (a large burial ground with tombs of religious figures and generations of pilgrims) of more than 2,000 monuments, including domed mausoleums and kulpytas, which are ornately carved stone steles traditionally used as Kazakh gravestones. The 12-chamber mosque is carved into the rock, and a shaft of daylight is cast onto two sacred wooden poles below. According to a local tradition, pilgrims recite a prayer and circle the poles three times counterclockwise, which is believed to help the spirits hear them. Visitors also tie strips of white cloth around the poles, the knot symbolically binding a prayer to the sacred site. These practices likely come from Shamanic and Tengrian traditions of tying strips of cloth to sacred trees and mountain passes to honor nature spirits––customs that became intertwined with local forms of Muslim saint veneration over time.

Nearby, a well offers pilgrims a much-needed respite; these sacred complexes grew around the few natural resources that made life in the desert possible.

Domed mausoleums at the Shopan-Ata necropolis.

The entrance to Shopan-Ata, shaded by a mulberry tree. These mosques were built around oases that sustained life in the harsh desert climate.

Legend holds that centuries later, Shopan-Ata appeared to Beket-Ata in a dream, offering spiritual guidance, making this shrine an important stop before continuing to Beket-Ata. Nearby, a well offers pilgrims a much-needed respite, its water an incongruous presence in a landscape this dry––a reminder that these sacred complexes grew around the few natural resources that made life in the desert possible.

The sacred wooden pole, around which visitors tie white cloth to seek blessings.

The final few stairs leading up to the Beket-Ata shrine.

Just over an hour away, Beket-Ata is perhaps the best-known of the five mosques. Founded by the 18th-century Sufi teacher Beket Myrzagululy, the shrine lies in a remote canyon about 170 miles from Aktau, the Caspian-side gateway to Mangystau. The steep descent into the canyon is a reminder that the effort needed to reach these shrines has always been a part of the devotion.

The structure is carved into the pale rock, its interconnected chambers following the curves of the cliff. Narrow openings in the ceilings pull shafts of daylight into the cool, dim rooms, where rugs are spread across the stone floor.

Communal dining is integral to Kazakh culture.

An imam is usually on hand to receive visitors and share information about the site. As we settle on the carpets, he details each of the chambers, one of which contains Beket-Ata’s grave, and another is associated with his sister. The remaining rooms are used for prayer, with separate spaces for men and women.

My pilgrimage continues into the dining hall, where a long, continually replenished table runs through the room, with pilgrims sitting on either side and eating together. The mosque provides some freshly cooked meat free of charge, while visitors leave bread, sweets, tea, yogurt, jam and other provisions for those who arrive after them—an especially vivid expression of Central Asian hospitality.

Next we drive across remote country to the Tyub-Karagan Peninsula for Shakpak-Ata, whose cruciform mosque is carved into a massive chalk cliff. Its porous white surface, which looks almost like honeycomb against the desert, was shaped millions of years ago when this part of Mangystau lay beneath the ancient Tethys Sea. Inside, drawings and inscriptions in Arabic, Persian, and Turkic—some dating back to the 18th century—offer a tangible record of the pilgrims who traveled here from across Central Asia, long before air-conditioned 4x4s and Starlink internet made traversing this unforgiving landscape simpler.

A honeycomb-like pattern along the rock face of Shakpak-Ata.

Slightly west, Sultan-Epe lies beside a deep canyon, where a stream threads through thickets of mulberry, buckthorn, blackberry, and wild herbs—another improbable pocket of green in one of Kazakhstan’s driest regions. Sultan-Epe is revered as a protector of seafarers and fishermen—a fitting association for a shrine overlooking the Caspian. According to local tradition, Sultan-Epe was the son of Hakim-Ata, a renowned Sufi poet and disciple of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, which connects the shrine to the spiritual tradition associated with Shopan-Ata and, through his later spiritual mentor, Beket-Ata.

The stacked-stone entrance to Sultan-Epe.

The final stop on the circuit is Karaman-Ata, where a seven-hectare necropolis stretches across a low, open plot of desert dotted with funerary monuments, some more than 1,000 years old. The mosque is carved into the slope of a small marl hill, and as you descend into the rock, the temperature drops noticeably from the heat outside. A narrow passage leads to a circular room believed to be associated with Sufi rituals including devotional whirling, a type of worship that is expressed through physical movement.

Karaman-Ata, the largest of the five rock mosques of Kazhakstan’s Mangystau desert.

Reaching each site still means long drives across remote terrain, with limited to no mobile coverage or fuel services–making a sturdy vehicle and a trusted local guide essential. But after days spent traveling the region, these places begin to alter your sense of the desert. Around a well, beneath a mulberry tree, or at a table crowded with food and strangers, the landscape that seemed so stark and inhospitable reveals an unexpected generosity, preserved in the rituals of those who continue to make the journey here.

#4913. Pain Prevalence Higher in Women, Increases Most Rapidly Before 55

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Women experience a higher prevalence of pain than men across different areas of the body, according to a large global study published October 5 in Nature Medicine.

The analysis, which included more than 6 million people, also found that pain prevalence generally increased with age, with the most rapid increases occurring before age 55.

The findings come as lower back pain, neck pain, and osteoarthritis — all common causes of pain — are projected to become more prevalent globally by 2050.

Pain, especially lower back pain, is the leading cause of disability worldwide. However, researchers have lacked a standardized way to examine how self-reported pain varies across the life span and different regions of the world.

This new study is one of the largest efforts to date to examine self-reported pain using a standardized approach.

The researchers analyzed data from 6,125,459 individuals spanning 118 countries from 1990 to 2025. Participants ranged in age from 5 to more than 100, and 55% were female.

They used self-reported data on pain across 11 body sites:

The researchers found that women consistently reported a higher prevalence of pain across all 11 sites than men.

The largest differences between women and men were in facial pain, headache, and stomach or abdominal pain.

Pain prevalence also increased most rapidly before age 55, especially at musculoskeletal sites such as the hips, back, and knees.

The researchers found that the prevalence of pain varied considerably by body region and differed by age.

Back pain was the most commonly reported, affecting 40% of participants, while facial pain was the least common at 2%.

Neel Anand, MD, a board certified orthopedic spine surgeon and director of the Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained some factors that may contribute to the high prevalence of back pain.

“Our modern lifestyles involve more prolonged sitting, less physical activity, and more time spent looking down at phones, tablets, and computers, all of which can contribute to poor posture and increased stress on the spine,” he said.

“As we get older, the discs between our vertebrae naturally lose moisture and elasticity, making them more vulnerable to degeneration, bulging, and herniation. Excess weight and smoking can accelerate this process,” Anand added.

In addition to pain at individual body sites, the researchers examined three broader measures: any bodily pain, high intensity pain, and generalized pain.

Any bodily pain was defined as pain reported at any site. High intensity pain was defined as an average pain intensity of 7 or higher on a 0–10 scale. Generalized pain was defined as pain occurring in 4 of 5 body regions according to the 2016 fibromyalgia spatial criteria.

The prevalence of any bodily pain increased progressively across the life span, from around 30% at age 5 to 70% among people ages 100 and older. All three pain measures were consistently higher in women than men.

While any bodily pain increased with age, high intensity and generalized pain peaked in mid-to-late life before declining.

High intensity pain peaked around age 50, while generalized pain peaked around age 70.

These different patterns could help identify when prevention and pain management efforts may be most beneficial across the life span.

Vernon Williams, MD, a sports neurologist and founding director of the Center for Sports Neurology and Pain Medicine at Cedars-Sinai Orthopedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline there are several signs that pain should be evaluated by a doctor.

“People shouldn’t feel that they simply have to live with pain. I especially recommend talking with a doctor when pain persists, interferes with sleep or daily activities, limits exercise or function, or is accompanied by symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness,” Williams said.

“Persistent pain deserves an evaluation to identify the underlying cause and develop an appropriate treatment plan.”

The researchers found that smoking, obesity, and lower household income together accounted for 18.3% of the global pain burden across all body sites.

People who currently smoked had a modest but consistently higher prevalence of pain across body sites from adolescence through age 65. The strongest association was seen with facial pain.

Obesity was increasingly associated with pain beginning in early adulthood, particularly in weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips, feet, and ankles.

Lower household income was also associated with a higher prevalence of pain across all body sites beginning in early adulthood. The strongest association was seen with chest pain.

People with the lowest household incomes were more than twice as likely to report chest pain as those with the highest incomes. This difference was greatest in midlife and narrowed at older ages.

Williams noted that medication isn’t the only option for managing pain.

“Regular, appropriately paced exercise can help change how the brain experiences pain, while mindfulness, breathing exercises, adequate sleep, and other behavioral strategies can help the nervous system better regulate the pain response,” he said. “When medication is needed, I encourage patients to discuss non-opioid and non-pharmacologic options with their doctor as part of a comprehensive approach.”

Anand added that, “The best strategy remains prevention and preservation of function: maintaining a healthy weight, strengthening the muscles that support the joints, and avoiding smoking can all help reduce the strain placed on the musculoskeletal system.”

#4911. The 6 Best Undereye Patches, Tested and Reviewed by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

The entire Women's Health team swears by them.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’m always up late doomscrolling TikTok and The White Lotus subreddit for season 4 theories. (AJ Michalka hive, stand up!) The only problem? Those late nights mean I have dark circles and puffiness in the morning (boo!). While I'm a huge fan of undereye creams, sometimes I get bored and need to switch things up. Enter undereye patches. They're a fast fix for dryness, puffiness, and dark circles—and even help me fake eight hours of sleep. "The skin under the eyes is prone to changes related to aging skin, such as fine lines, and conditions like dryness and discoloration," says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. In just 10 to 20 minutes, undereye patches temporarily hydrate the delicate skin and help me look refreshed. Plus, they're super cute and add a fun touch to my selfies, even if they're shared to just my Close Friends circle on Instagram Stories.

Like any other skin care product, eye masks really get their power from their ingredients, some of which are typically hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, and caffeine.

“Eye patches incorporate key ingredients like hyaluronic acid to boost moisture, peptides to firm, ceramides to strengthen the skin barrier, caffeine to help reduce puffiness, and niacinamide to reduce discoloration,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD.

As with any beauty product, there are always a few things to consider before making the investment. Since these masks are mostly advertised for their ability to soothe and hydrate, you'll want to check the hydrating and firming ingredients, and keep your expectations realistic since results are usually temporary. Here's what to look out for.

For starters, look for key ingredients such as aloe, chamomile, cucumber, green tea, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid. You're less likely to come across vitamin C and retinol, but it's a plus if you do. Patches with a cellulose gel material can also prevent them from sliding off your face (a con I often deal with and try to avoid as much as possible).

Not only is the skin under your eyes thinner and more delicate than in other areas of your face, but it’s also where lymphatic fluid drainage occurs, says dermatologist Lauren Penzi, MD. It can also show more blood vessels, and in turn, make dark circles appear more visible, says Dr. Garshick. Most eye masks are created to reduce fine lines, undereye darkness, and wrinkles while giving your skin the boost of moisture it needs. The overall effect of these patches is to revive and hydrate, which is why so many people use them to get a more refreshed look.

Many people complain about looking tired, and eye patches are a nice, quick fix. Still, it's important to be realistic about the kind of results you'll get in just one or two uses. So, you’ll want to zero in on the reason you’re buying patches, says Dr. Camp. For example, you can target puffiness by rocking undereye patches infused with caffeine or green tea while getting ready for work, says Dr. Camp.

As a member of the beauty team at Women’s Health, I’m constantly on the hunt for the best products and spend a lot of my time testing and reviewing the latest drops. I frequently consult skin experts, which is exactly what I did to kick off my selection process here. I consulted five New York–based dermatologists and had them give their recommendations with insight on why these undereye masks are so splurge-worthy. Then, I tested several of their picks and compared them to some of the other undereye masks available in our beauty closet.To narrow down the list even further, I got a few other members of team WH, including Addison Aloian, Lily Wohlner, Brian Underwood, and Danielle Jackson, to get in on the testing process. Ingredients, price, and overall efficacy were taken into account to determine which would be best for a wide range of needs and preferences.Here are the fruits of our labor.

After testing tons of undereye masks, this one takes the cake for best overall. Why? It's the most hydrating option on this list and it doesn't slip off your face, which is super hard to find in an undereye mask.

ICYMI, Wander Beauty basically started the undereye mask trend. This OG mask is made with peptides, amino acids, and hyaluronic acid to improve your skin's texture, tone, and hydration. It's also expert-approved by Dr. Garshick and dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "I love that this mask is made with three different layers that allow the formula to penetrate the skin deeply and prevent it from sliding off the face, so you can multitask while you wear it," says Dr. Engelman.

Wander Beauty patches are as effective as they are Instagrammable. I’ve been a fan of the rose gold and yellow gold patches for five years, and all of my beauty editor friends gush over them. They brighten, hydrate, and plump up my fine lines. They also contain calendula extract and aloe vera to help reduce puffiness. Ahem, hi holiday parties and upcoming travel—I’m looking at you.

These pretty patches have three unique layers: the surface's foil retains heat and prevents evaporation, the middle grips to prevent slippage, and the base delivers moisturizing glycerin and de-puffing calendula extract. For an extra soothing experience, I like to leave mine in the fridge. Cool temperatures help shrink blood vessels under the eyes, so dark circles appear lighter and puffiness minimizes, dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, said in our guide to undereye skin care.

That said, the construction of this mask consists of super light and flexible material versus the conventional plastic material found in a lot of other eye patches that were tested, giving this product a high-quality feel.

I would be remiss if I didn't mention my personal fave patch from Patchology. It contains hyaluronic acid (hi, hydrated, plump skin) and feels super cool under the eyes to de-puff and smooth out that area.

Patchology is fantastic for targeting lines, says dermatologist Anar Mikailov, MD. He mentions that there's resveratrol, a natural antioxidant found in grapes that helps improve barrier function, and other antioxidants that provide protection against oxidizing agents that can visibly age the skin by causing wrinkles. There’s also antioxidant-rich strawberry extract, which helps brighten dark circles.

After using this patch, I also noticed my undereye area was less puffy and more luminous. My only con was that the mask slides out of place after a while, but it’s still epic to use and totally worth incorporating into your routine. My hack is to use these patches while lying down in bed to prevent any slipping.

This undereye mask is basically an expert at reducing puffy, tired-looking eyes thanks to its cooling effects. It also temporarily plumps up my fine lines with hydrating hyaluronic acid.

This option comes with a lot of serum, so it may slip down your face over time. But, feel free to go ahead and massage that extra serum into your undereye area—that little bit of massaging can help assist with lymphatic drainage and further reduce puffiness. Need even more convincing? Celebs like Jessica Alba post about this mask on her Instagram story time and time again, noting that she's a major fan.

Most masks on this list only need 10 minutes on the skin, but this one should stay on for up to 20. Although, 20 minutes fly by when you have a good book in hand (pro tip!).

These eye masks from Live Tinted are packed with copper peptides and banana extract (hi, Ashton Hall!) to reduce puffiness and smooth fine lines. They also reduce puffiness after just a few uses and leave skin looking glowy and feeling hydrated.

And because these patches help soften and smooth your delicate undereye area, Aloian relies on them for makeup prep. "Not only is the patch super cute—it's shaped like a sun—but it also genuinely hydrates and brightens my undereye area," she says. These patches make Aloian feel confident going makeup free because of the glow they leave behind, but it's just as helpful on days when she wants a dewy base before applying concealer.

Along with a mix of peptides to help stimulate collagen production, this eye mask contains niacinamide, bakuchiol, caffeine, and vitamin C. Bakuchiol is a great retinol alternative that helps stimulate collagen production, says Dr. Mikailov.

Wohlner also gave this patch a try and loves how flexible it is under the eye. However, she did note that it does tend to slip down the face because it's super thin.

This vitamin C-packed eye patch is perfect for helping brighten up the undereye area while reducing signs of aging and puffiness with the help of caffeine.

Yeah, it's a little pricier, but trust that it's totally worth it if you have the budget. The gel patches are super easy to apply. Plus, they can reduce discoloration and fine lines within just a few weeks. Sometimes I'm wary of products with vitamin C in them because the smell can be a bit aggressive, but these are just right.

Derms also deem this patch worth the money. "The key ingredient in this mask is THD Ascorbate Vitamin C, which is 50 times more powerful than other forms of vitamin C," says Dr. Engelman. THD is especially good for surface dark spots that need brightening rather than deeper dark circles, says Dr. Mikailov.

It's worth noting that these dry up around the 10-minute mark, and while they stay on really well, the edges break off easily if you try to move the masks around a few minutes after the initial application.

As the name suggests, this patch is meant to soothe tired-looking eyes. So, for those of you who have a lot of sleepless nights or are just night owls at heart, this is your winner. Infused with caffeine, niacinamide, and hyaluronic acid, these work overtime to reduce puffiness and dark circles.

"I often recommend Peace Out’s acne patch for the face, but I also love the brand’s eye patches," says Dr. Engelman. "It's so effective at quickly bringing down puffiness and brightening and smoothing the under-eyes." The patch is biodegradable and made with biocellulose, which helps the formula deeply penetrate the skin, says Dr. Engelman.

These patches fit snugly under my eyes, so I could wear them while doing my eye makeup. They also did a great job of catching eyeshadow fallout that would normally ruin my undereye concealer. Another pro? Unlike most gel patches, they weren’t completely soaked in serum, which can make the process a bit messy. Instead, they had just the right amount for ample hydration. After the initial use, I noticed my undereyes were softer and brighter, and I’d slowly reach for these patches for special occasions.

I’m not the only fan on WH’s beauty team. “I have very sensitive skin, so I'm always cautious when it comes to trying things out, but this didn't give me any issues,” says tester Sabrina Talbert. “It also doesn't have much of a scent, which put my mind at ease since fragrance tends to be an early indicator that my skin might not like a product.”

These patches are on the larger side, so they feel a bit bulky. They also need to be slightly adjusted because they slide down a little bit over 15 minutes, but honestly, they’re such minor cons that Talbert continues using them.
