#4888. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

You can send Micah tips at Micah@electrek.co, or find him on Twitter, Instagram, or TikTok.

#4887. 8 Best LED Face Masks in 2026, Tested by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

Our top picks—from Therabody, Omnilux, and CurrentBody—bring doc-approved technology to your home.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As our beauty editor, I’m often asked by my friends about LED face masks. Do they actually work? The short answer is yes, but there are some caveats. These devices use various wavelengths, with red light being the most popular option to help stimulate collagen production for plumper, less wrinkled skin over time. Blue light is commonly used to target acne and green LEDs target dark spots, says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD. A 2018 study suggests that LED light can even help support wound healing and treat inflammatory skin conditions like psoriasis.

Even the best LED face masks won’t do much if they’re collecting dust in the back of my closet. I actually need to be committed to using my new device regularly. I see the best results when I use my CurrentBody Skin 2 Face Mask for 10 minutes, three times a week. When I stop for several months, I notice my complexion is duller and hyperpigmentation from acne is slower to fade.

And sure, these light therapy tools might resemble the infamous mask from The Phantom of the Opera, but I don’t mind. The minor trade-off of temporarily looking like I haunt the Paris Opera House is worth it because my results speak for themselves. I’ve been using mine consistently for eight years, and my face is noticeably clearer, even-toned, and radiant.

While I’ve been a fan of LED face masks since 2018, they can get pricey (think $300 and up). Given the upfront cost, it's important to do your research and find one that will truly tackle your unique skin issues, ensuring the investment is worthwhile. If you do, the device will pay for itself, and see your skin through the hormonal acne caused by your period and the fine lines that can affect your skin during menopause.

I’ve tried dozens of LED face masks since 2018. If there’s one light therapy device I won’t part with, it's the CurrentBody Skin 2. It ticks all my boxes for a light therapy tool, such as emitting multiple wavelengths to boost my glow. A trio of red, near-infrared, and deep near-infrared wavelengths delivers more anti-aging benefits than a single-wavelength treatment.

My skin glowed after the first 10-minute treatment, and my hormonal acne disappeared in two days. Within the first month, my skin’s radiance improved, and hyperpigmentation and fine lines were less noticeable. Consistency is key with CurrentBody: the more often I use this mask, the better my skin looks. Whenever I stop, my skin looks duller in a few weeks. Even sporadically, I see improvement in acne, dark spots, and lines.

CurrentBody Skin also comes with a bunch of accessories to elevate my at-home skincare experience. My favorite is the optional protective eye inserts, which let me watch TV while my skin clears up.

Lately, I’ve been trying to bring the hotel spa vibes to my apartment, and using this mask helps enhance my mood. Hear me out: I like to power on my Philips Hue lamp, turn on a spa playlist, and just close my eyes and try to clear my thoughts for the day. Admittedly, it was initially a challenge to sit there and just attempt to zone out, but after a week, it became easy to follow and a seamless way to mellow out.

My favorite upgrade in the Series 2 mask is the addition of a chin strap. Our jawline and chin often show skin laxity and aging, similar to a line of demarcation when wearing the wrong foundation color. The chin strap provides extra coverage where my hormonal acne occurs and helps calm inflammation.

Since I’m so into this face mask, I wanted to share a quick comparison among CurrentBody Skin and a few of our reader-favorite picks, including Omnilux, Dr. Dennis Gross, and Therabody.

CurrentBody Skin vs. Omnilux: Both use red and near-infrared wavelengths, have the same number of LED bulbs, and are made from flexible silicone. CurrentBody also uses deep-infrared light to reach wrinkles. It includes a chin strap, while Omnilux does not.

CurrentBody Skin Vs. Dr. Dennis Gross: Our team loves Dr. Dennis Gross products, including the face steamer and chemical exfoliant. However, the sturdy hard-shell design is best suited to Eurocentric features, while CurrentBody’s flexible silicone material accommodates a wider range of facial features.

CurrentBody Skin vs. TheraFace: TheraFace offers greater facial coverage, but it lacks a chin strap. Like CurrentBody, it emits red and infrared lights and provides blue light for anyone dealing with acne. This is a surprise issue that women in their 40s often face due to perimenopausal and menopausal symptoms. TheraFace also vibrates to relax facial tension and boost circulation around the eyes, brow line, and scalp, but it’ll set you back $650.

Read More: Best Red Light Therapy Devices For Hair Growth

Okay, $299 isn't exactly cheap, but Qure's mask is the least expensive option on our list by a few bucks, and if you're on the hunt for a mask that checks all of the boxes (who isn't?!), here's your answer. In addition to two types of red light—red and deep red—for anti-aging benefits, the mask also features infrared, amber, and blue lights to address acne, fine lines, and sunspots. Select your skincare concerns, and a compatible smartphone app will customize a treatment plan just for you. The icing on the cake? Treatment time is only three minutes for all plans—among the fastest of all the devices we tested.

We love that the Qure sits squarely on the face so it won't need to be constantly readjusted (an annoying feature of some of the others we tried). That being said, our testers told us it isn't heavy or cumbersome. "This mask is lightweight and fits my face perfectly, making me feel like I am reaping the most benefits," says Earley.

On the downside, the customization component made things overly complicated, says Metzger, who tested this mask for three weeks. "In theory, the smartphone app is cool and useful—and some people will probably really enjoy this feature—but I found tinkering with it to be too time-consuming and defeated my favorite aspects of simplicity and speed," she says. "Also, I want full-face anti-aging, so the regular setting works just fine."

Admittedly, it's a little tricky to get the eye protection into the mask at first (even after reading the directions, Metzger inserted the removable eye protection in the wrong way), but a quick tutorial video solved the problem.

We previously named this our favorite LED face mask in our 2023 Beauty Awards. Solawave has since given the device a major revamp, including bumping up the LED count by over 140%—it initially had 132 LEDs compared with the 320 today. The silicone mask is now covered from edge-to-edge in light-emitting diodes to ensure my entire face is covered.

The brand also added two wavelengths. Beyond the standard red and near-infrared LEDs, there’s now amber and deep red lights that penetrate deeper into the skin for more visible results.

But my favorite improvement is definitely that the original 10-minute treatment is now only 3 minutes, making it seamless to incorporate into my daily routine. Don’t worry: It doesn’t skimp on quality. The combination of cycling through four wavelengths helps supercharge the potential skin benefits.

After charging and cleansing her face, fitness editor, Cori Ritchey, CSCS, put this LED face mask to the test. The Ulike is her first-ever red light therapy device, but she found it comfortable to wear and easy to use. Ritchey says the hardshell design doesn’t leave redness or marks on her face. Instead, there is plush padding around her eye area and a cushiony, adjustable head strap that stays in place throughout her back-to-back treatments.

Ulike stands out for its four pre-set LED treatments. She can safely stack two treatments to customize your session to your specific skincare needs. Here’s a quick look at the different modes:

Glow brightens dull skin with a combination of yellow (590 nanometers), red (630nm), and far infrared (830nm) wavelengths. A 2025 randomized controlled trial found that when yellow lights at 570nm and 590nm are combined with red and infrared light, they effectively improve photoaging caused by the sun and tanning beds. The trial also found this combo helps reduce pores, wrinkles, texture, and brown spots.

Firm mode boosts collagen production for plumper skin and reduce wrinkles with a mix of red (630nm) and far-infrared (830nm) wavelengths.

Rejuvenate combines yellow (590nm) and far-infrared (830nm) wavelengths to help calm her skin and target hyperpigmentation.

Clear emits a trifecta of blue (465nm), red (630nm), and far-infrared (830nm) wavelengths. In our guide to blue light therapy, dermatologists appreciate the shorter wavelengths—ranging from 400 to 500nm—to help kill acne-causing bacteria called C.acnes.

After three weeks of testing, Ritchey says it’s comfortable, easy to incorporate into her minimal routine, and capable of improving her skin. She’s new to red light therapy, but found this device to be a solid investment for newbies. While not an overnight skin fixer, Ulike Reglow provides a healthy radiance that helps justify the cost, especially when it’s on sale. It’s helpful if you want to achieve and maintain a long-term glow if you’re willing to use it consistently. It pays off by helping to keep your skin clear, though it’s still relatively early in the game for Ritchey to speak on its anti-aging benefits.

The makers of WH’s award-winning Theragun changed our team’s skincare routine when they entered the beauty tools market in 2022—and we’re still fans. This hard-shell mask features a 9-minute preset mode that cycles through these LED lights:

Red light stimulates collagen and firms skin. Red plus infrared to boost circulation for a more even skin tone. And blue to battle acne-causing bacteria.

You can also enjoy a quick 3-minute mini treatment using just one of the above modes. So yes, this one is a bit on the pricey side, but it's a lifelong purchase—you can use it through years of younger-you breakouts to whenever you first start to see the signs of aging. FWIW, it’s equipped with 648 medical-grade lights, which is more than most competitors.

Underwood used this face mask for several weeks, and absolutely noticed a difference in his skin. His go-to mode was the nine-minute preset treatment with the vibration, which leads him through three minutes of each light type. “I felt like this was the best bang for your buck, and I noticed a huge brightness boost as well as far fewer breakouts,” says Underwood. “I usually have an odd spot or two on my face, but I really didn't notice anything while I was using this." He even did a few sessions with the lights off and just enjoyed deep breathing during the vibrations, which made for major relaxation. Talk about the ultimate spa-worthy splurge!

Honkus reviewed the TheraFace Mask and agrees it’s worth the luxurious price tag: The brand recommends using it for at least 12 weeks to see results, but she saw results in just three weeks. "Any zit that was brewing under the surface of my skin calmed before it reached the surface, my eyes appeared less tired, which I attribute to the vibration function, and my skin looked more luminous than usual,” said Honkus. “I’m confident that with continued consistent use, the results will become more striking."

On the downside, both Underwood and Honkus say this mask is on the heavier side and can be a bit cumbersome to wear. The cordless design helps since they can lie down while using the device. And though Therabody doesn't specify the nanometers of light used, it’s an FDA-cleared device with a 12-week clinical study showing notable results, so you can trust that this one is actually effective.

Dermatologists Shari Sperling, MD, Sherwin Parikh, MD, Brendan Camp, MD, and Dr. Garshick all rave about this mask, which improves sunspots, age spots, and discoloration while helping with current acne and future breakouts. "Using a combination of red and blue light, this mask works to support collagen production as well as reduce acne-causing bacteria and inflammation," says Dr. Garshick.

But not only is this mask recommended by dermatologists, it was developed by one too—that'd be Dr. Dennis Gross, founder of his eponymous skincare line. That could be why it's so effective and user-friendly.

"I’ve been using the DRx SpectraLite FaceWare Pro consistently for about three weeks and I found it was much easier to incorporate into my routine than I'd initially expected," said longtime beauty editor and writer Lisa DeSantis, who tested the device for a month.

Since incorporating this mask into her routine, DeSantis noticed less irritation, a more even-toned complexion, and smoother skin "I trust that with continued use, I may even start getting ID’ed at bars again,” she said. “If you do have acne-prone skin, a mask like this one could yield more visible results as you’ll be able to tell if you’re experiencing fewer breakouts or improved healing time."

Dr. Dennis Gross has the potential to be a best overall pick, but it’s pricey and the hardshell mask is less likely to fit different face shapes and features. For those who prefer a hard mask, the adjustable strap in the back can make for a more comfortable experience.

Dr. Dennis Gross DRx SpectraLite FaceWare Pro Review

We’ve tested dozens of face masks, and this one is ideally suited to tackle lines and acne scars. It's simple, but it gets the job done fast. "I just plug it in while I'm lying in bed and let Omnilux do its thing for 10 minutes—that's all you need to get the job done,” says Wohlner.

She also raves that the mask works wonders on her skin. Wohlner uses this device three times every week and she has seen quick results. “My skin looks clearer and brighter, and it has an overall glow like I've never experienced," she says. As someone with hyperpigmentation and acne scars, Wohlner says the mask reduces the severity of her imperfections when she uses it a few times a week. The red light is also helpful for mature women with wrinkles or those with facial redness.The mask sits comfortably and closely on the face, so you don’t need to push it into your skin for extra benefits. Also, keep the included box and pouch to protect your mask from accidental damage and dust. Since Wohlner doesn’t have pets or kids, she tucks her mask under the bed. But if you’ve got mischievous loved ones, you can place it out of their reach, like in your standing desk drawer, closet, or on the top shelf of your dresser. Ultimately, just pick a spot you have quick, easy access to.If adult acne is a non-issue, then lucky you! You’ll totally love this face mask for anti-aging benefits. However, if you deal with the occasional zit or pimple rearing its ugly head, but you also don’t want to compromise on anti-aging, then opt for another model like the TheraFace that combines both blue and red lights.

The biggest plus of the MZ Skin LED Mask is its simplicity—you can master the two settings without reading the instructions. Though not equipped with many of the bells and whistles of CurrentBody Skin and TheraFace, this MZ Skin mask is highly recommended by plastic and reconstructive surgeon Jaimie DeRosa, MD, because it also offers different types of light—red, infrared, and blue—and multiple settings.

The anti-aging mode helps firm your skin by stimulating collagen production with red light, while the acne mode uses blue light's antibacterial properties to clear skin. While it's the priciest option on our list, the device is well-designed, with a luxe vibe that makes you feel like you're using a very high-end treatment. It’s also the prettiest of our editor-approved recommendations.I first tried the gold MZ Skin Mask in early 2019 and appreciated the five modes, but mainly used the blue light to minimize acne. LED face masks are hands-free, so you can wear one while on your phone, reading, or watching TV. Here’s what to know when purchasing the best LED face mask.

Most at-home red light therapy devices use a mix of red and blue wavelengths. However, each LED shade offers different benefits, so you’ll need to find the right color for the skin concerns you want to treat, says dermatologist Leah Ansell, MD. Here’s a quick guide:

Standardized wavelengths are helpful, but the number of lights is also important, says dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD. A higher concentration of LED bulbs provides more even coverage.

Not all LED face masks are built the same.

My favorite light therapy masks are made from flexible materials like silicone, but it ultimately comes down to your personal preference and what you’re more likely to use consistently. I’ve noticed an immediate glow since using these devices, but more noticeable results take about four to six weeks. So you're going to want a face mask you can stick with.

Carving out time for self-care in your busy schedule can sometimes feel like a stretch. Thankfully, these LED face masks require a relatively low time commitment. LED face masks are usually class II devices. They’re either FDA-listed or FDA-registered, meaning the brand notified the agency about the device. However, this listing doesn’t indicate the products are approved, cleared, or authorized by the agency.

They could also be FDA-cleared, meaning they are similar to other devices that are legally marketed for the same use. Our editors prioritized testing face masks that are either FDA-listed, -registered, or -cleared. And I referenced the FDA database to verify the status of our recommendations.

Yes, it’s generally low-risk for most users, says dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "LED light therapy is not an invasive treatment, and when done properly, the risks are minimal," she says. #4886. The 9 Most Walkable Cities in the US

Anyone who’s been to the pump lately could appreciate a little less reliance on cars. And while life in the most walkable cities in the US can mean saving on gas (not to mention car insurance, parking, and potential parking tickets), getting around on foot isn’t only about your budget. Walkability “can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” says Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, which has been following and analyzing walkability for years with their Walk Score tool. “There’s also a housing-market component: People tend to value the convenience and access that comes with living in a walkable neighborhood, and that desirability can translate into high home values. Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors,” says Fairweather.

To determine the country’s most walkable cities, we’ve reviewed recent studies, like the one from Only in Your State, a travel and discovery platform, plus talked to realtors, residents, and tourism experts across the country.

Hoboken is located on the banks of the Hudson River.

Just across the Hudson River from Manhattan, Hoboken is the most walkable city in the US, according to Only in Your State’s most recent analysis. The one-square-mile-city earned a nearly perfect Walk Score of 97, thanks to its dense street grid, many mixed-use buildings, and abundance of public transportation. Three other cities in the Garden State also cracked the list’s top 10: Union City, West New York, and Jersey City.

Though LA isn’t known for being particularly pedestrian friendly, West Hollywood remains a walkable enclave.

Los Angeles County isn’t known for its public transit, but even so, West Hollywood snagged the fourth spot in Only in Your State’s analysis, earning a Walk Score of 91. The city packs over 300 restaurants, bars, and coffee shops into just under two square miles. West Hollywood’s walkability is especially prized because the area is one of LA’s most vibrant nightlife districts, creating safe accessibility for revelers on the world-famous Sunset Strip.

In addition to being one of the country’s oldest, Boston is also one of the most walkable cities.

“What makes Boston special is that every neighborhood has its own personality and you can experience so much of the city on foot,” says George Sarkis, CEO and cofounder of the Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman. “You can walk from the historic brownstones of Beacon Hill to the boutiques and restaurants of Back Bay, through the Public Garden, and into the South End without ever feeling like you’re covering much ground.” Walking is the best way to truly enjoy all of the city’s historic sites, centuries-old architecture, and cobblestone streets.

San Francisco’s hilly landscape can turn a casual stroll into an all-in workout.

This Bay Area city has one of the highest transit scores in the country, making it a breeze to go car-free. But for many locals—like Wendy Newman, a realtor with Wesely & Associates and a resident since 1987—walking is the real experience. “​​In one outing, you can buy groceries, stop for coffee, admire a Victorian’s unreasonable paint palette, nod at the neighbor whose face you know but whose name you still haven’t learned, and discover a bookstore you weren’t looking for,” she says. Plus, San Francisco’s mild climate makes taking a spin through neighborhoods like Chinatown and North Beach enjoyable year round.

New York City is built on a grid system, making it easy to navigate.

Just about every expert we talked to mentioned NYC, a metropolis made for a good stroll. From the café-lined lanes of Little Italy to particularly scenic stretches like the East River Promenade and Brooklyn Bridge Park, the Big Apple is big on pedestrian access. And the city’s high walkability score has benefits beyond just saving on cab fare, points out Kate Wollman-Mahan, a real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate New York. “Life expectancy in New York City is five years longer than the national average, according to the city-run Health Dashboard and economist Jonathan Miller (82.3 years versus 77.3 years),” she says. “Walking is built into everyday life, from going out to coffee to running errands to walking in the park.”

A stroll around DC can take pedestrians past national monuments and charming townhouses.

According to Walk Score, a research platform that promotes walkability, DC has a walk score of 98. It's such a popular pedestrian playground that even local cultural institutions embed walking into their education approach. Take the Spy Museum, for example, which developed its own free walking tour because of the breadth of strolling space in the area and interest from both residents and tourists. “We send them around the National Mall and downtown area with espionage history that happened in those exact places throughout history,” says Aliza Bran, the museum’s director of media relations. Other particularly walkable neighborhoods include Dupont Circle, U Street, Capitol Hill, and Georgetown.

The Windy City is a certified walking city.

The Windy City tops the US ranking for walkability from Preply, a language learning marketplace that runs walkability studies across the US, Europe, and Asia. “You can walk between Chicago’s five most-visited attractions (the Art Institute, Millennium Park, Cloud Gate, the Chicago Architecture Center, and the Magnificent Mile) in 28 minutes, about 2,500 steps,” says Preply’s communications leader Madeline Enos.

Sheldon Bishop, the founder of BrewAtlas, a guide to independent specialty coffee shops, argues that the best sign of a walkable neighborhood is a good cafe. And Chicago is particularly well caffeinated, thanks to 95 specialty cafes across 41 neighborhoods. “When people can walk to get coffee, they run into neighbors, stop into the bookstore next door, and spend money on the block instead of at a drive-thru,” he says.

Miami is full of walkable pockets, according to local residents.

For Sandra Masis, director of sales at the residential building Arbor Coconut Grove, it’s neighborhoods like Coconut Grove that make Miami such a pedestrian-friendly city. “You can walk to restaurants, cafés, shops, parks, and the waterfront, all while enjoying the neighborhood’s lush greenery and relaxed atmosphere,” she says. “It has a sense of community that makes you want to get outside and explore.” And Miami’s newer developments, like Brickell, prioritize walkability as much as older neighborhoods like Coconut Grove and Little Havana. “Even in a city built around cars, you can create pockets where people can comfortably live, work, and socialize on foot,” says Masis.

Contemporary high-rises mingle with historic sites in Philadelphia.

Every year GuruWalk, a platform for free tours, puts together a ranking of the best cities in the world to explore on foot. In their most recent study, NYC took the top spot among US cities, and Philadelphia came in just behind it. GuruWalk’s Carolina Martínez says that though Philly gets fewer visitors than other places on the list, those who explore it love it. “Philadelphia has a 4.99 average rating, with 99 percent of reviews at five stars,” she says. “Walk a few blocks through the historic district and you’re standing in front of Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell.” New Orleans, San Francisco, and Boston round out the top five.

#4885. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4884. I Work Out for a Living—Here Are the Best Headphones for Everything From Runs to Gym Sessions

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Because every sweat session needs an epic soundtrack.

WHETHER YOU PREFER to listen to music, a podcast, or tune into sports while getting your sweat on, you'll need a solid pair of workout headphones to make it happen. Beyond a high-quality pre-workout, nothing elevates your training quite like the perfect pair of headphones. These devices not only drown out grunting gym-goers but also help you stay focused, find your rhythm, and push through those last few reps when your body is telling you to quit.

The key to a good pair of workout headphones is finding ones that fit your ears snugly and won't budge while you run or do kettlebell swings. Workout headphones need water resistance to handle sweat and 5-mile runs in the rain. We can recommend eleven pairs of workout headphones for a range of training environments.

Like our favorite running shoes, modern workout headphones are built for performance, combining durability with athletic-minded features. Sweat and water resistance are non-negotiable, while a secure, comfortable fit prevents them from falling out during burpees, sprints, or heavy lifts. Meanwhile, battery life has improved dramatically in recent years. Many models offer enough juice to power through a week’s worth of workouts on a single charge. Need to focus? Noise cancellation, intuitive controls, and quick-pairing technology keep you in the zone rather than fumbling with your tech.

Whether you’re just starting your fitness journey or a seasoned athlete, the best workout headphones can transform your training sessions. The Men’s Health fitness and tech editors tested a few dozen options to identify the eleven best models available. From true wireless earbuds to over-ear models to bone conduction headphones, these top-performing headphones deliver impressive durability, high-quality sound, and workout-specific features to help you push through the pain.

The AirPods Pro have improved significantly over the past few updates, and the latest version, the AirPods Pro 3, is what we believe are the best do-it-all workout headphones. These earbuds deliver excellent comfort, premium features, and high-quality sound. Apple has systematically addressed every pain point we experienced with earlier models, transforming these wireless earbuds from casual earbuds into essential fitness companions.

The fit is a major reason the AirPods Pro work so well during workouts, even surpassing the latest Apple release, the Apple AirPods 5. After dozens of reps, we found they don’t budge. The multiple silicone ear tips let our testing team find the perfect seal during burpees and box jumps. Despite wearing them for multiple training sessions (and in the office), we experienced no ear fatigue thanks to their lightweight design.

The improved ergonomics also contribute to better passive noise isolation, working with active noise cancellation to block out excessively loud gym music. For athletes who rely on music for motivation during workouts, the secure, comfortable fit eliminates the constant annoyance of loose earbuds that need readjusting. Their IP57 rating provides additional peace of mind, ensuring they can handle the sweat that comes with serious workouts.

MH Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, found the most exciting new feature of the AirPods Pro 3s to be their ability to monitor your heart rate through your ear canals, a capability more commonly associated with devices that wrap around your wrist or chest. They aren't the first headphones to do so, but having this added to Apple's already impressive offerings only strengthens their case.

Battery life exceeded our expectations, with up to eight hours of continuous playback and a charging case that extends total listening time to 24 hours. The case supports wireless charging, making it easy to recharge on a charging pad. Meanwhile, the AirPods Pro 3 support several advanced features like adaptive audio, conversation awareness, and transparency mode, the latter of which lets outside sound in, so you can be aware of what’s going on around you during a run.

The touch controls are intuitive during workouts—you can play/pause, skip tracks, answer a call, and adjust the volume by pressing the stem. For iPhone owners, the AirPods are a cinch to set up. Simply open the case next to your phone, tap Connect, and you’re ready to go. This combination of comfort, performance, and ease of use makes the AirPods Pro 3 the best overall workout headphones, setting a high bar for others to match.

While the Beats Studio Pro aren’t specifically designed for working out, they’re by no means out of place in a gym. The headphones maintain the sleek, recognizable Beats aesthetic and bass-heavy sound the brand is known for, while offering premium features that make them great for training and office use.

The over-ear design provides top-notch sound isolation through plush memory foam ear cushions, while the adjustable headband distributes weight evenly across your head. They balance comfort with stability—the headband applies just enough pressure to keep the headphones secure without becoming uncomfortable during extended wear. During testing, the Studio Pro remained firmly in place through moderate workouts like weightlifting and walks, though they’re not ideal for high-impact exercises.

Battery life is fantastic, lasting up to 40 hours with ANC off (24 hours with ANC on). When the battery gets low, you can get up to 4 hours of playback with just 10 minutes of USB-C charging. However, features like spatial audio and dynamic head tracking are exclusive to iPhone owners.

That said, the Studio Pro omits some features that are standard on other premium models, like ear detection, so they don’t automatically pause the music when you remove them from your head. Still, the headphones provide impressive performance wrapped in the brand’s iconic style.

Setting up these headphones was a breeze, with the same seamless iPhone connectivity you’d expect from AirPods.

The previous model’s ear hooks felt awkward, but the new design is much more comfortable, with five different ear tip sizes for a secure fit. During testing, these headphones felt glued to our ears—even during a windy run—and didn’t flinch after getting drenched in sweat thanks to the IPX4 rating. The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 holds the top spot among the best bone conduction headphones and was featured in the 2025 Men’s Health Tech Awards, so it’s no surprise they’re a favorite here.

Even in noisy environments like busy streets or gyms, we didn’t have to max out the volume to hear our favorite tunes. In addition to its lightweight design, the headphones offer up to 12 hours of battery life and an IP55 rating, so they’ll hold up to your toughest workouts.

Setup is straightforward, with quick pairing with both Android and iOS devices, and a Bose Music app that lets you customize EQ settings and update the firmware. The improved noise cancellation is particularly impressive, effectively blocking noise. Touch controls on each earbud are responsive without being overly sensitive, and the conversation detection feature automatically pauses music when you start speaking.

Battery life is around eight hours with ANC enabled, with the case providing an additional 30 hours. A quick five-minute charge delivers about one-and-a-half hours of listening time in a pinch. Overall, the Buds Pro 2 are the best wireless earbuds for Pixel phone owners, offering excellent comfort, sound quality, and durability. Plus, you get powerful features like Live Translate and Gemini support, making them more than just workout headphones.

Android users have no shortage of options, including those on this list. But Samsung’s extremely lightweight Galaxy Buds 3 Pro stand out, offering excellent features and performance for everyday use and workouts. Their AirPods-like stem design is more comfortable and secure than the Buds 2 Pro, with silicone ear tips (available in 3 sizes) that create an effective seal without causing discomfort during extended wear. They’ll stay firmly in place through running, HIIT workouts, and strength training sessions.

The IP57 rating provides excellent protection against both dust and water, making these earbuds capable of surviving temporary submersion up to 1 meter. If you like to rough it while working out, these earbuds are durable enough. The Galaxy Buds 3 Pro earbuds also deliver high-quality sound, with an adaptive mode that blends ANC based on your surroundings. These features work seamlessly, so you can hear important sound cues like sirens more easily.

Powerful voice controls elevate the hands-free experience, letting you manage playback, adjust volume, and toggle between listening modes without a specific wake phrase—simply say “volume up,” and the earbuds will increase the volume. While these earbuds get just about everything right, they lack true multipoint connectivity, meaning they can’t maintain simultaneous active connections to multiple devices. However, Samsung users benefit from Auto Switch technology, which automatically transitions the earbuds between your Galaxy phone, tablet, and laptop whenever you start media on a different device.

For people whose ears tend to reject standard earbuds, the Powerbeats Fit offer a secure alternative with its flexible wingtips and snug, workout-friendly design. While the unusual fit takes some getting used to, our testing found the buds stayed put during HIIT, running, strength training, and everyday use.

"They're still the finest, and steadiest fitness earbuds out there," says Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. "The latest iteration doesn't change too much of the (very effective) formula they've had, which is just fine because they work so well."

Fit can vary by ear shape, and one of our testers initially experienced soreness from the wingtips—an issue that eased with shorter wear times and a switch to smaller ear tips. Once adjusted, the seal improved both comfort and sound quality. The wingtips effectively prevent slippage during intense workouts, though you need to place them carefully to keep them secure.

Sound quality is strong for workout earbuds, with active noise cancellation and transparency modes that are easy to toggle in the app, though not quite as robust as the AirPods Pro. Controls are simple, with identical tap functions on each side, plus handy features like auto-pause and magnetic charging-case guidance. The 30-hour battery life is a major advantage.

We were a little bummed that the box doesn't include a USB-C charging cable or on-earbud volume control. While other headphones with ear hooks may feel even more secure, the Powerbeats Fit offers a compelling blend of stability, sound, and battery life. At $200, they’re a worthwhile pick for anyone who needs earbuds that reliably stay put during tough workouts.

Read More: Our Full Review of the Powerbeats Fit

Open earbuds let outside noise in by design, but that same openness can make it hard to hear your audio on a busy street. The Shokz OpenFit Pro tackles this with a triple-microphone array and adaptive algorithm that dampens outside noise without sealing your ear canal. It won’t replace full ANC, but it quiets things just enough that you can actually enjoy what you’re listening to. Sound quality has also improved over previous OpenFit models, with better bass response and zero distortion at higher volumes.

The soft silicone ear hooks sit behind your ears, keeping the buds stable during runs and listening sessions—and because of the open-ear design, you stay aware of your surroundings the entire time—a real safety advantage over traditional earbuds. Battery life is solid, too, stretching 12 hours without noise reduction and extending to 50 hours total with the case.

JBL has always known how to do bass, and the Endurance Race 2 lives up to that reputation. The 6.8mm dynamic drivers deliver a low-end that’s full and punchy without overpowering the mids, which is exactly what you want when a heavy playlist is the only thing getting you through a final set. JBL’s Twistlock wing design twists into your ear, keeping them in place during jumping exercises.

The IP68 rating means these can handle full submersion, not just sweat. ANC and Smart Ambient mode let you toggle between blocking out the gym and staying aware of traffic on a run. Battery life tops out at 12 hours per charge, with the case extending that to 48 hours total. That’s enough to last a long weekend without needing to find a wall outlet.

If you go hard during your workouts, you'll sweat—probably a lot. You need headphones that can keep up. Look for headphones or earbuds that are at least water-resistant or, even better, waterproof. Really, earbuds usually offer better sweat resistance than over-ear headphones. Over-ear headphones with sweat-resistant construction are a lot harder to find, although brands like Sony and Beats still hold up well to sweat. If most of your workouts are moderate, sweat resistance may not matter, and any pair of the workout headphones we've noted below will work for you.

Your favorite gym clothes aren't the only things drenched in sweat after a workout. So durability for workout headphones starts with water and sweat protection, measured by the standardized Ingress Protection (IP) rating system. The rating has two numbers: the first indicates dust protection (6 being the highest), and the second indicates water resistance (9 being the highest).

For serious athletes (and seriously sweaty workouts), we recommend headphones that offer water protection to survive intense training sessions. If you primarily work out indoors, you can get by without dust protection, but consider proper dust resistance if you’re trail running or doing HIIT on the beach. Beyond dust and water resistance, the best workout headphones boast impact-resistant materials, such as durable plastic, high-grade silicone or rubber, and reinforced hinges and headbands.

Comfort and fit are essential for peak performance. While these factors can be highly personal, certain features separate the headphones you’ll love wearing from those that’ll end up at the bottom of your gym bag.

Several types of workout headphones suit different preferences. In-ear models are the most popular for workouts thanks to their compact size, and they come in several variations. The first type features interchangeable silicone tips in small, medium, and large sizes, creating a customized seal in your ear canal. Another design incorporates flexible ear hooks that loop over your ears for added stability.

If you don’t like wearing earbuds, on-ear headphones provide cushioned pads that rest against your ears, while over-ear models create a complete seal around each ear. Bone conduction headphones offer a unique solution by conducting sound through your cheekbones while keeping your ear canals open. These are a good option for anyone who needs to maintain awareness of their surroundings, such as when running at night or in a busy city.

When you’re crushing a grueling rowing routine or leg day, the last thing you want is your headphones dying mid-workout. Look for wireless earbuds that provide at least six to eight hours of continuous playback, or on-ear/over-ear headphones that can go 20+ hours on a single charge. That should last through a full week of workouts.

The good news is most earbuds come with charging cases that can extend total battery life by several hours; it’s like having a portable battery with you at all times. Additionally, features like wireless charging and fast charging make it even more convenient to keep your headphones powered up, whether you’re dropping them on a charging pad before bed or need a quick boost before heading out the door.

Obtuse controls can throw off your entire rhythm, so look for earbuds and headphones with simple buttons or touch controls. The best workout headphones feature intuitive controls that let you skip tracks, adjust the volume, and answer phone calls—all without touching your phone. Some headphones even offer customizable controls through companion apps, allowing you to tailor the experience to your needs.

Connectivity should be equally seamless. That means pairing quickly with your smartphone without jumping through menus and Bluetooth settings. For instance, the AirPods Pro 3 and Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are easy to pair with an iPhone—simply open the earbuds’ case near your device and tap to connect. Once paired, your AirPods can automatically connect to all your Apple devices through iCloud. Android users can take advantage of Fast Pair technology, which offers a similar one-tap connection experience with compatible headphones.

Additionally, many models now support multipoint pairing, allowing you to seamlessly switch between your phone and computer without manually disconnecting and reconnecting your headphones each time. Voice assistant integration adds another layer of hands-free convenience, letting you control your music, set a timer, or make a phone call using just your voice.

For those of us who work in busy offices, active noise cancellation (ANC) can be a game-changer for blocking out distractions. In gyms, this technology is just as useful, drowning out clanking weights, loud conversations, and blaring music.

However, the best workout headphones don’t just block out noise—they also let noise in. For outdoor workouts (or simply walking down the street), a transparency mode is an essential safety feature that uses the headphones’ microphones to pipe in ambient noise, such as approaching vehicles and emergency sirens. The most effective models let you switch between ANC and transparency modes with a simple tap or voice command.

Beyond noise cancellation, adaptive audio can automatically adjust the sound based on your environment, so you don’t have to constantly fiddle with volume controls.

For the past six years, Men's Health's fitness and tech editors have been testing dozens of the top workout headphones for men. Experts, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, and Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, have put countless options through the paces in multiple workout types to evaluate their fit, durability, comfort, sound quality, and price throughout all of it.

The testing environments included, but weren't limited to, busy CrossFit boxes, elite performance facilities, mountain trails, garage gyms, and outdoor tracks. We even wrote this story while testing various models to listen to podcasts, tunes, and even books in a busy work environment.

The guide below highlights what we believe are the best workout headphones to know about right now.

Sweat causes a lot of wear and tear on over-ear headphones, especially the ear pads. We recommend using only over-ear headphones for moderate activity, such as lifting and light cardio. You don't really want to wear over-ear headphones for HIIT or other high-cardio workouts, because the more sweat you create, the more likely your headphones are to slip and slide around on your head.

Over-ear headphones do provide great sound quality, and if you are strategic about how you work out with them, you likely won't see sweat as an issue until much farther down the road. In one specific case, one of our editors was a big fan of his Beats Studio Pro headphones for weight lifting. It took about 3 years for his ear pads to wear down from sweat and regular use, so he then bought replacement ear pads for those headphones.

You won't have any problems with sweat and water resistance on the running headphones we curated above; however, some are rated higher than others—which means they're more durable.

When you see an "IP" rating, what you are really reading is the Ingress Protection rating. You can read a rating from each number: the first indicates dust protection, and the second indicates water protection. Some of the headphones above have an "X" as the first number. The X indicates that no data were collected on dust protection. Sometimes it helps to know the dust protection, especially if you're running on trails. If you're a trail runner, it's probably worth paying attention to the more rugged running headphones that also have a dust rating.

The second number indicates how waterproof the headphones are. Zero is the lowest, while 9K is the highest (you're unlikely to see a 9K rating on headphones because this level is reserved for materials that can handle direct, high-temp, high-pressure water).

So what's a good number range to look for? We recommend anything between four and six, but seven and higher is a premium rating and can withstand full submersion in water. Most of what you will see is "IPX4", which is solid, but if you're really wanting a pair of running headphones that are made to handle high activity, then look for a second number of seven or above.

#4883. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4882. Inside the Governor’s Mansions That Will Soon Be Home to 19 Newly Elected Leaders

In January, the United States’ 19 newly elected governors won’t just have inauguration day on their calendars, but moving day, too. All but five states have governor’s mansions for their leaders to live and work from, with the exceptions being Arizona, Idaho, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont. These executive residences tend to be grand in style and scale, often possessing a long, rich history—even some haunted ones.

Sometimes, governors forego their official residences in favor of privately owned homes. For example, California governor Gavin Newsom recently listed the $7.5 million Fair Oaks home he lived in instead of the official executive residence, a 19th-century Victorian in Sacramento. Montana’s governor’s mansion is currently empty and in disrepair, while a governor hasn’t inhabited the official residence in Nebraska in over a decade.

Most states, however, have longstanding traditions of their leaders living in their official governor’s mansions. Virginia has the oldest continuously inhabited executive residence—every governor has lived there since 1813. If our new league of governors opts for tradition, here’s where they will be resting their heads for the next few years.

Republican Tommy Tuberville won Alabama’s gubernatorial race and will be able to move into a 119-year-old mansion in Montgomery following his inauguration. Built in 1907 by architect T. Weatherly Carter, the 17-room neoclassical residence features a row of four Corinthian columns at its front entrance, which opens to a foyer with a grand bifurcated staircase.

California’s new governor-elect is democrat Xavier Becerra, who will soon reside at a three-story Victorian in Sacramento. Built in 1877, the 20,000-square-foot house was thoroughly renovated in 2015, decades after Ronald and Nancy Reagan’s brief stint living there in 1967 before deeming it uninhabitable. The mansion was then used as a museum until its 2015 update, when it became home to the state’s governors once again. It has 30 rooms, Italian marble fireplaces, original wood floors, and a kidney-shaped swimming pool.

In Denver, democrat Phil Weiser will receive the keys to the red brick governor’s mansion known as Colorado’s Home. Built in 1908, it has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1960. The Colonial Revival–style home has 27 rooms and shares its one-acre grounds with gardens, a historic gazebo, a greenhouse, and a carriage house. Thanks to John Hickenlooper, governor from 2011 to 2019, the home also has a rotating selection of local beers on tap.

Republican Byron Donalds just made history as Florida’s first Black governor. The state’s Greek Revival–style governor’s mansion in Tallahassee was completed in 1956 on the site of the original governor’s mansion built in 1907, which had fallen into disrepair. A screened swimming pool, a greenhouse, and a rose garden are among its amenities.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has the distinction of being the first Black woman governor-elect in the United States. Her soon-to-be residence in Atlanta is a 30-room Greek Revival mansion that was built in 1967 by architect A. Thomas Bradbury. Across three levels, it measures in at 30,000 square feet.

Iowa’s governor’s mansion, known as Terrace Hill, will soon be home to democrat Rob Sand. Dating all the way back to 1869, Terrace Hill is an 18,000-square-foot Second Empire–style residence in Des Moines where Iowa’s governors have lived since 1976. Its first two floors are open to the public as a museum and events space.

Democrat Hannah Pingree will move into the Blaine House in Augusta, Maine. Originally built in 1833 in a combination of Federal and Greek Revival styles, the mansion has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1919, when renovations gave it a more Colonial style. It has 28 rooms across two stories, including a billiards room. The property also hosts a formal garden and a tennis court.

In Michigan, democrat Jocelyn Benson has the good fortune of governing a state with two official executive residences: one in the state’s capital of Lansing, and an official summer residence on Mackinac Island. The former is a 1957-built 8,700-square-foot ranch-style home with five bedrooms and four bathrooms; the latter is an Arts-and-Crafts-style mansion that was built in 1901.

Democrat Amy Klobuchar, currently a US senator for Minnesota, won her state’s gubernatorial election and will move into a 16,000-square-foot residence in St. Paul that dates to 1912. It features seven bedrooms, 10 bathrooms, and nine fireplaces. Architect William Channing Whitney designed the stone-and-brick dwelling in a combination of English Tudor and Beaux-Arts styles.

Nevada also elected its first Black governor, democrat Aaron Ford, who will soon reside in a Classical Revival–style mansion designed by architect George A. Ferris in 1909. It features a grand entrance hall, a reception room, a formal dining room, a governor’s study, and a luncheon room, in addition to private living quarters.

New Mexico’s governor-elect, democrat Deb Haaland, has made history as the first Native American woman to hold that title. In Santa Fe, the governor’s mansion is referred to as The People’s House. Designed by architect W.C. Kruger, the midcentury-modern structure was completed in 1955.

Democrat Amy Acton will be Ohio’s next governor, granting her residency inside a 1925 mansion in Bexley, just outside of Columbus. The Tudor-style home was built by architect Robert Gilmore Hanford, and its grounds boast three acres of extensive gardens, including a “Storybook Trail” inspired by The Tales of Peter Rabbit.

Republican governor-elect Mike Mazzei will be the new steward of Oklahoma’s official governor’s residence in Tulsa. The 14,000-square-foot Dutch Colonial was built in 1928 and has a limestone façade that matches the State Capitol building two blocks away. Uniquely, its grounds boast a swimming pool shaped like Oklahoma, an outdoor kitchen, and a tennis court on the former site of a helipad where President Lyndon B. Johnson landed in 1964.

Helena Foulkes, a democrat, won the race for Rhode Island’s governor, but she isn’t necessarily going to move out of her current residence any time soon, since the state doesn’t have an official governor’s mansion. Foulkes owns two homes in the state: a $3.8 million eight-bedroom summer house in Narragansett and a $2.3 million three-bedroom home in Providence.

Republican governor-elect Alan Wilson won South Carolina’s vote, making his next home a two-story Federal-style mansion dating back to 1855. Originally used as military academy officers’ quarters, it has been the official governor’s residence since 1868, three years after the Civil War ended. Inside, it has a central entrance hall connecting to two drawing rooms, a state dining room, and a library. Private living quarters are located on the second floor.

Marsha Blackburn, the Republican governor-elect of Tennessee, can move to a 10-acre estate in Nashville’s Oak Hill suburb. Known as Far Hills for the surrounding picturesque views, the three-story Georgian-style mansion was built in 1931. It has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1949.

In Texas, democrat Gina Hinojosa will be the first Latina to hold the state’s highest office. Her official residence will be a Greek Revival–style mansion in Austin. Spanning nearly 10,000 square feet, it has been home to Texas’s governors since it was built in 1856.

Democrat David Crowley won in Wisconsin, making him the first Black governor of the state. The state’s executive residence is a Classical Revival–style mansion located in Madison. Completed in 1928, it has 16,000 square feet of interior living space across three floors, including seven bedrooms, 13 bathrooms, seven fireplaces, and 10 gardens.

Republican Eric Barlow will soon have access to the governor’s residence near Frontier Park in Cheyenne, Wyoming. In 1976, it replaced the state’s former executive residence, which was built in 1905 and is now open as a museum. Available details of the current mansion are sparse, however, and it seems that a new, upgraded version with improved security and functionality may soon be in the works.

#4881. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.
